item.title: REVIEW: Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Acer Predator Atlas 8 review: Potent performance at a slightly better price Thanks to its Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you get top-notch graphics for $350 less than its closest rival. Modern handheld PCs started out as complimentary devices, compact systems designed to help you game on the go when you didn't have access to your beefy setup at home. But as the category has matured, we've seen manufacturers pursue higher tiers of performance. This culminated most recently in systems like MSI's Claw 8 EX AI+, which delivers serious graphics power along with an equally serious price of $1,800. But now, Acer is trying to undercut the current framerate champ with the Predator Atlas 8, equipping it with the exact same chip used in MSI's machine, but for $350 less. The result is a compelling package that delivers on many of the same highs while easing the burden on your wallet. With the Predator Atlas 8, Acer hasn't strayed too far from the basic template we've seen on so many other portable PCs. The middle of the system is dominated by a large 8-inch LCD TFT display with a 120Hz refresh and respectable 500-nit brightness. On the outside you get TMR analog sticks along with an Xbox-style button layout. I must admit I'm not a huge fan of Acer's circular D-Pad as it's a bit mushy and doesn't feel super precise. But if you're not playing fighting games or similar titles, it's more than serviceable for navigating menus. And if I'm really nitpicking, colors from the Predator's TFT screen aren't quite as rich as what you get from MSI's machine, but it's the kind of difference that you only really notice when you look at the two systems side by side. Around back, Acer included a pair of rear paddles, two shoulder buttons and analog Hall-effect triggers with plenty of travel — the latter of which are great for racing games. Along the top edge of the system you get all of the Predator Atlas 8's ports, which includes dual USB-C jacks with support for Thunderbolt 4, a microSD card reader for expandable storage, a 3.5mm audio jack and a power button with a built-in fingerprint reader. All told, it's a pretty standard setup, though the Predator does lack a USB-A port like you get on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. I also noticed that while Acer's dual two-watt speakers can get surprisingly loud, audio becomes distorted at higher volumes (above 50 TK) that results in a crackly or crunchy sound. That said, the speakers are so punchy, I found that I never really needed to turn them up that high. Unless you're trying to DJ a house party with this thing, you might not even notice. The real star of the Atlas 8 is its Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor, which is the exact same chip used in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. The main difference is that Acer's handheld comes with 512GB of storage instead of 1TB and tops out with 24GB of shared memory (compared to 32GB on the MSI). This discrepancy almost entirely accounts for the price gap between the two systems. But for people striving for top-notch performance while trying to save a few bucks, the framerate delta in games isn't as pronounced as you might think. When I tested this out in Cyberpunk 2077 at 35 watts on FHD, medium graphics and XeSS set to performance, the Predator Atlas 8 hit 88 fps, which is barely more than five percent lower than the 95 fps I got from the Claw 8 EX AI+. But it's important to note that this was using Acer's highest performance mode. When I set the system to 15 watts (which you might do when playing on battery only), the Predator and the Claw were essentially dead even in Returnal at FHD and medium graphics (60 fps for the Acer vs 59 fps for the MSI). This means that if you're trying to decide between the two, you really need to consider how you plan on using your handheld and what types of games you'll be playing. Similar to other high-end Windows handhelds, the Atlas 8 comes with Microsoft's Xbox experience. This software allows you to boot into a dedicated UI for gaming instead of needing to deal with the traditional desktop OS. This also makes it super easy to download all of the most popular launchers and storefronts like Epic, Steam, Battle.net and more, and because it's Windows underneath, you get better compatibility than what you get from SteamOS-powered portables. That said, if you're the type to travel with a portable monitor, keyboard and mouse, you can still switch over to the classic Windows interface to get some work done too. The Atlas 8 is powered by an 80WHr battery that provides ample longevity, though it can vary quite a bit depending on what you're playing. However, without even doing anything to boost its longevity, I was able to play World of Warcraft: Forever at FHD on medium settings for an hour and 45 minutes on a single charge while still keeping frame rates consistently above 90. On the flipside, when I played a less demanding title like Warhammer Survivors, Acer's machine had more battery life than I knew what to do with: It lasted for more than three hours before needing to be plugged in. Notably, both of those games were played using the handheld's 30-watt Balanced performance mode, so if you're not afraid to mess around with its settings, there's a lot of room to tweak this thing to get even longer untethered gaming sessions. I'm still not sure how I feel about PC handhelds that cost well above $1,000. For me, that's just a ton of money to drop on a system that can't multitask as well as a similarly priced gaming laptop. However, for mobile gaming enthusiasts trying to find the sweet spot between price, performance and portability, Acer has carved out an interesting niche with the Predator Atlas 8. At $1,450, it costs $350 less than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, while sporting the exact same processor and delivering essentially 95 percent of the performance. That said, Acer's more approachable pricing leaves the Predator with a bit less RAM and storage, though having a microSD card slot provides a workaround for the latter. There are also some minor differences, like the lack of a USB-A port, a slightly less colorful TFT display and speakers that sound a bit wonky at high volumes. But these shortcomings could very well be a worthwhile trade-off for anyone looking for peak handheld gaming performance without completely fragging their budget.

item.title: REVIEW: Hisense UR9 review: How close can RGB Mini LED get to OLED?
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“The Hisense UR9 is one of the most ambitious TV's on the market.”
- Excellent backlight control with very little distracting blooming - Impressive HDR brightness and rich, saturated colors - Native 180Hz panel with 4K 120Hz console gaming support - Surprisingly capable 4.1.2-channel Devialet sound system - OLED still offers better absolute contrast and viewing angles - Some blooming remains in challenging scene The Hisense UR9 is one of the most ambitious televisions the company has released, bringing RGB Mini LED technology to a more mainstream 65-inch model. Unlike conventional Mini LED televisions, which use a white LED backlight, the UR9 uses individual red, green, and blue LEDs to produce light and color. The promise is greater brightness, richer colors, and more precise backlight control, all while retaining the brightness advantages of LED technology. On paper, it sounds like an impressive combination, and the UR9 certainly has the specifications to support those ambitions. With a claimed peak brightness of 3,500 nits, 980 local dimming zones, and a native 180Hz panel, it’s positioned as a premium television with plenty to offer. More importantly, its performance in some areas is genuinely impressive, particularly when it comes to backlight control and HDR. But with its price putting it directly up against some of the best OLED TVs on the market, does the UR9 offer enough to justify its position? Let’s take a closer look. Hisense UR9 looks and build: A clean design with a practical stand Hisense has kept the UR9’s design fairly understated. Slim bezels frame the display, and the dark metallic finish gives it a neat, clean appearance. The construction feels solid, although the television is noticeably thicker than many premium OLED models. At approximately 4.5 centimeters, it isn’t particularly slim, but the overall design is tidy and functional. I particularly like the centrally mounted pedestal stand. Its relatively small footprint makes the UR9 easier to position on narrower TV furniture, while two height adjustments give you some flexibility if you plan to place a soundbar underneath. Small perforations around the television also house speakers for the integrated Devialet audio system. The UR9 looks good and feels well built, but its design leans more towards practicality than luxury. For a television in this price category, I would have liked to see a more premium finish. Hisense UR9 display performance: RGB Mini LED delivers excellent backlight control The UR9’s biggest selling point is its RGB Mini LED display. Conventional Mini LED televisions use a white LED backlight, with additional display layers producing the colors you see on screen. Hisense takes a different approach, using individual red, green, and blue Mini LEDs to produce light and color directly. The idea is to deliver a wider color range, greater brightness, and more precise control over the picture. Compared with the more affordable UR8, Hisense has pushed the specifications further. The UR9 features a claimed peak brightness of up to 3,500 nits, 980 local dimming zones, and a native 180Hz panel, all powered by the company’s Hi-View AI Engine RGB processor. It’s an impressive specification sheet, but the more interesting part is how well the television puts that hardware to use. Mini LED televisions can struggle with blooming, particularly when bright objects appear against dark backgrounds. The UR9 does an excellent job of keeping this under control. Watching 1917, bright white text against a dark background looks clean, blacks appear deep, and there’s very little distracting glow around highlights. Consistency is another part of the experience I appreciated. Some Mini LED televisions can exhibit flickering, brightness fluctuations, or noticeable changes in backlight intensity as scenes transition. The UR9 generally avoids these issues. It delivers a stable picture, and at times, you almost forget you’re watching a backlit television. Blade Runner 2049 is another good demonstration of what the display can do. Dark scenes have impressive depth, shadow detail is excellent, and colors, particularly reds, look rich and beautifully saturated. Brighter HDR content brings out the television’s other strength. Highlights have plenty of punch, colors look intense, and there’s a cinematic quality to the overall presentation. Even in brighter scenes, the image looks vibrant without becoming excessively processed. There is still a distinction between the UR9 and a flagship OLED, however. The television does an excellent job controlling blooming, but a backlit display cannot eliminate it completely. In particularly challenging scenes, such as the starfield in Alien: Romulus, some glow remains visible around brighter objects. The difference becomes more apparent when you compare it with OLED. Each pixel on an OLED panel can be controlled independently and switched off completely, giving the technology an advantage when producing perfect blacks and controlling highlights. The result can also look more three-dimensional. The UR9 comes surprisingly close in many situations, but OLED retains the edge in absolute contrast and viewing angles. RGB Mini LED is getting remarkably close to OLED in certain areas, but it hasn’t completely closed the gap. The UR9 makes a strong case for the technology, particularly when it comes to backlight control and brightness. Hisense UR9 audio output: Devialet makes a difference to the built-in sound Hisense has partnered with Devialet to give the UR9 a 4.1.2-channel speaker system. That’s an ambitious setup for a television, particularly when you consider how slim most modern sets are. The system includes dedicated up-firing speakers, along with support for Dolby Atmos and DTS. The audio presentation is surprisingly spacious. Watching movies, there’s a good sense of width and height, with sound extending beyond the physical boundaries of the television. Bass has decent depth, and the speakers maintain their composure even at higher volumes. There are a couple of areas where I’d like to see improvement. Action scenes could use more punch, while dialogue doesn’t always have the clarity and presence I’d want. I also found that Theatre Mode can make voices sound a little too distant or echoey. Standard Mode is the one I’d stick with for most content. Even with those shortcomings, this is one of the better built-in television sound systems I’ve come across. I’d still recommend a dedicated soundbar for a proper home theater setup, but it’s good to see Hisense putting this much effort into the onboard audio. Hisense UR9 software: Google TV keeps the smart experience familiar The US version of the UR9 runs Google TV, which is a good fit for a television in this category. You get access to major streaming services, including Netflix, Disney Plus, Prime Video, and YouTube, along with a wide selection of additional apps through Google Play. The interface is familiar and relatively easy to navigate, with personalized recommendations based on what you enjoy watching. Google Assistant voice capabilities are included, and there are plenty of options to customize the viewing experience. There’s nothing particularly unusual about the smart TV experience here, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Navigation is straightforward, the app selection is extensive, and most viewers should feel right at home with Google TV. 180Hz gaming and useful connectivity options Gaming is another area where the UR9 is well equipped. The native 180Hz panel is an interesting addition, particularly if you’re planning to connect a gaming PC. Hisense includes three HDMI 2.1 ports, support for 4K at up to 180Hz, Variable Refresh Rate, and Auto Low Latency Mode. It’s been upgraded to handle a massive 4K signal at up to 180 Hz depending on whether content is SDR or HDR, and can push to 330 Hz variable refresh rate for gaming, depending on your resolution There’s also a DisplayPort connection, which isn’t something you typically find on televisions. It’s particularly useful for PC gamers looking to take advantage of higher refresh rates. The main compromise is the number of HDMI connections. You get three ports rather than the four available on some competing televisions, which could be limiting if you regularly connect multiple consoles and other devices. Input lag is less impressive. Testing measured approximately 32.5 milliseconds at 60Hz in standard Game Mode. Enabling the Refresh Rate setting brings that figure down to around 24.6 milliseconds. Both results are perfectly usable for casual gaming, although they’re not particularly impressive compared with dedicated gaming displays. For everyday console gaming, the UR9 still offers a good feature set, especially with its support for 4K at 120Hz. It has the features most console players will want, while the higher refresh rate and DisplayPort connection give PC users a little more to work with. Lower US pricing makes the UR9 more compelling Pricing makes a significant difference to the UR9’s appeal. When Hisense originally announced the television in the US, the 65-inch model was expected to retail for around $3,500. By the time it reached store shelves, however, the company had brought the price down to approximately $1,999. The revised price puts it in a much more interesting position. Here’s how the US pricing breaks down: - 100-inch: Originally announced at $8,999 Additional discounts are already making the 65-inch model more attractive, with prices dropping to around $1,700 at certain retailers. The UR9 brings together flagship-level RGB Mini LED technology, impressive brightness and backlight control, a 180Hz panel, and a surprisingly capable built-in sound system. Hisense is making an aggressive play in the premium TV market, and the lower price makes the television easier to recommend. OLED remains a major competitor, particularly with options from LG and Sony available at similar prices. Even so, the UR9 has a stronger argument in the $1,700 to $2,000 range for the 65-inch model. It brings some genuinely impressive display technology to a lower price point, without necessarily requiring buyers to spend flagship OLED money. The combination of RGB Mini LED, impressive brightness, and a capable feature set makes the UR9 a compelling option in the premium TV category. Should you buy? The Hisense UR9 is one of the most interesting televisions to come out of the company, and a genuinely impressive demonstration of what RGB Mini LED can achieve. Its backlight control is arguably the biggest achievement. The ability to produce deep blacks, minimize blooming, and maintain consistent contrast is impressive for a backlit television. There’s plenty more to like, too. The UR9 gets incredibly bright, delivers rich HDR performance, and has a surprisingly capable built-in sound system. Its gaming features also make it a well-rounded option, particularly if you want a television that can handle both console and PC gaming. OLED still has the advantage in a few important areas. Perfect blacks, wider viewing angles, and that extra level of depth and dimensionality in the picture remain difficult for a backlit television to match. Price is another important consideration. At around $2,000 in the US, the UR9 makes a lot more sense, but OLED is still difficult to beat if you’re spending flagship-level money. RGB Mini LED is heading in an exciting direction, and the UR9 shows just how far the technology has come. It might not be the OLED killer just yet, but it’s certainly one of the strongest arguments for what RGB Mini LED could become. Why not try? The UR9 makes a strong case for RGB Mini LED, but OLED remains worth considering if perfect blacks and pixel-level contrast matter more to you. A conventional Mini LED option is also worth a look if you’re interested in comparing how different backlight technologies handle color and contrast. LG C6 OLED: If you’re more interested in OLED’s pixel-level contrast, the LG C6 is an alternative worth considering. It offers the kind of perfect blacks and precise highlight control that the UR9 still can’t fully match. It’s the more natural choice if those aspects of picture quality matter more to you than the UR9’s brightness advantages. Samsung QN80H: The Samsung QN80H is another option if you’d rather look at a conventional Mini LED television. In some of the color comparisons from our UR8 testing, the Samsung produced bolder-looking colors. It offers a useful point of comparison if you’re weighing RGB Mini LED against a more traditional Mini LED approach. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) How is an RGB MiniLED panel different from a regular MiniLED TV? On an RGB MiniLED panel, each LED uses three independent red, green, and blue diodes to create color directly from the source, helping it achieve wider color gamut coverage, better tones, and sharper contrast control. Is it good for gaming? Yes. In addition to a fast panel with a 180Hz refresh rate, you also get support for Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro. How well does it handle glare? The Obsidian Panel allows it to minimize ambient light artifacts, retaining deep black even in daylight. What about the software? It runs Google TV with Gemini built in, enabling features such as conversation search, while providing access to thousands of apps and plenty of free channels. Is the audio output good? The Hisense TV comes equipped with an 80W, 4.1.2 multi-channel surround sound system tuned by Devialet with Dolby Atmos support. Bass has decent depth, and the speakers maintain their composure even at higher volumes. What video modes are supported? It can handle Dolby Vision, IMAX Enhanced, and Filmmaker Mode. For lower-resolution content, there’s also support for AI 4K and HDR upscaling.

item.title: REVIEW: Lenovo ThinkBook Plus 14 (Gen 7) Auto Twist review: Amazing that it exists, but you shouldn't buy it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Name a show or conference where technology and automotive companies gather, and you're likely to find a smorgasbord of cutting-edge concepts and fanciful experiments that normal consumers will never have the opportunity to buy, let alone use. Lenovo is one of the few companies that regularly brings at least a few of its most creative ideas to market, and many of those experiments manifest in the Lenovo ThinkBook Plus family. The most recent addition to the lineup is a laptop that attaches its display with a complex 2-axis motorized hinge, allowing the display near-complete vertical and horizontal freedom to follow you wherever you go. It's a fascinating idea, and Lenovo's iconic ThinkBook hardware is as solid as ever — but there are enough concerns and burning questions here that only a minuscule number of people should even consider buying this laptop. Lenovo ThinkBook Plus 14 (Gen 7) Auto Twist - Intel Core Ultra 5 325 (8-core) I'll be the first to praise Lenovo for continuing to experiment with interesting laptop designs and technologies, and I love that the latest ThinkBook Plus exists. The Auto Twist does have some intriguing ideas, too, and most of the core hardware is expectantly excellent — but that's not enough to forgive the half-hearted execution, higher price tag, and potentially compromised reliability. Ultimately, no one but the most affluent or passionate tech enthusiasts should realistically consider this laptop. - ThinkBook's industrial designs never fail to impress - Bright, responsive, and versatile OLED display - The 2-axis motorized display hinge can be cool - You're paying extra for a few questionably useful features - Motorized hinge does not instill durability confidence About this article: Lenovo provided the ThinkBook Plus 14 (Gen 7) Auto Twist unit for this review. The company did not have any input into this article, nor did it see its contents prior to publication. The Lenovo ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist is, at the time of writing, only available in the same configuration I reviewed, which retails for $2,199 with an 8-core Intel Core Ultra 5 325, 32GB of memory, and 512GB of storage. Apart from its display and memory, the ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist's specs feel decidedly mid-range, making its price stand out even more compared to something like the Lenovo ThinkPad T14 (Gen 7) I reviewed. It does make sense that you're paying a premium for the unique display features, and I have already seen the Auto Twist go on sale for as low as $1,899. Even then, that's a lot to pay for any laptop. - Display (Size, Resolution) - OLED, 30-120Hz VRR, 500 nits (SDR)/1,100 nits (HDR), Dolby Vision & DisplayHDR True Black 1000, glossy, multi-touch - 2x Thunderbolt 4 (40GBps, DP 2.1, PD), 2x USB-A (10GBps), 1x HDM 2.1, 1x 3.5mm audio - 4x stereo speakers, 4x microphone array, Dolby Atmos tuning The Auto Twist doesn't have enough "auto" for me I see Lenovo's vision, but Lenovo didn't push the envelope enough Every Lenovo ThinkBook Plus is defined by its "gimmick," so I won't beat around the bush. This year, Lenovo released the Auto Twist with a 2-axis motorized hinge that allows the display to open/close vertically and rotate horizontally. Combine that with the 10MP infrared-supported camera to track your position, quad-microphone array, and dual-speaker soundbar, and you get the ultimate display for presenters and movie watchers that can move with you... in theory. In practice, the experience leaves a lot to be desired. At least the issue doesn't lie with the screen itself. Lenovo outfitted the seventh-generation ThinkBook Plus with a 2.8K, 120Hz, 14-inch OLED panel that's delightfully crisp, smooth, responsive, and color accurate. It also gets plenty bright for practically every lighting condition, and the viewing angles are strong enough to deal with all the odd positions this display is liable to be in. There's also an ambient light sensor for automatic brightness and color correction, but I didn't notice it kick in nearly as often as it probably should have. As for what this laptop's headlining feature is capable of, there's a modest list of features. You can press the side-mounted power button to have the Auto Twist automatically open itself; you can press a hotkey in the function row to toggle "auto tracking," letting the Auto Twist follow your movements to keep the screen centered on you; you can open the Plus Center application to enable voice tracking with various commands, register yourself as a user with facial recognition so the Auto Twist will only track you, and access a handful of settings; you can manually move the display into a variety of positions. Vertically, you get about 180 degrees of adjustment, which is perfectly fine, but horizontal rotation is oddly limited — just over 180 degrees to the left, but only around 90 degrees to the right, so you also have to keep in mind what direction you move around the Auto Twist. Either way, you get three primary postures: traditional laptop mode, a "share" mode that faces the screen outward, and tablet mode that inverts the display and closes it. There's no way to switch between modes with the press of a button, but you can use the voice commands with the "Hi, Tiko" wake word to do so... which is convenient when they actually work. Even when they do, there can be odd glitches, like the Auto Twist not reorienting the display properly when you go from tablet mode to laptop mode. When you rely on the inconsistent auto-tracking feature, be prepared for the Auto Twist to regularly lose you before its slow, choppy motorized hinge can keep up — and tracking only worsens in low-light settings. The setting to have the Auto Twist close itself when shutting down or going into hibernation never reliably worked, either. More fundamentally, there's a real concern about long-term durability, and you'll regularly have to manually manipulate the Auto Twist's display, which is always accompanied by an off-putting whirring. Even when closed, the horizontal rotation is never locked, so the lid can shift and slide over the keyboard. Outside the display, it's (almost) all classic ThinkBook This laptop doesn't bet everything on its display gimmick The motorized display does add some weight and thickness, but Lenovo kept the penalty down while also delivering the ThinkBook experience we all know and love. The industrial aluminum chassis feels rock solid apart from the motorized hinge, and the weight is well-balanced despite the heavier display. You get a healthy array of ports for all your connectivity needs, including two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two full-sized USB-A ports, and an HDMI 2.1 port. I do wish Lenovo had put one Thunderbolt port on the right for more convenient charging and docking, but that's a minor complaint. The keyboard is typical Lenovo excellence with an intuitive layout and comfortable typing action, but the backlighting isn't particularly strong, and the function row keys are tiny to accommodate the two additional hotkeys for the display features. The mechanical touchpad is also smaller than many other 14-inch laptops because the display hinge shifts everything down. Even with its compact dimensions, though, the touchpad is responsive and premium-feeling. I appreciate having a fingerprint sensor in the power button (in addition to the Windows Hello facial recognition), but the power button lies almost flush with the laptop frame, so I constantly missed the target when trying to sign in. That's the end of my nitpicks, fortunately, as Lenovo delivered with its accurate and sharp 10MP webcam, the microphones are clear and do a good job of capturing your voice even from a distance, and the quad speakers (split between the base and display) deliver a wide, full soundscape for a 14-inch laptop. Aggressively mid-range internals can hold you back You're paying a lot for the display, not the performance or endurance Aside from 32GB of quick, soldered memory, the ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist boasts a rather unassuming specs sheet. It's powered by an 8-core Intel Core Ultra 5 325, and the single M.2 2280 slot is filled with a fast-but-small 512GB SSD. That's not a lot of power for $2,000, but the ThinkBook Plus admittedly does run incredibly smoothly with typical workloads. To get the numbers out of the way, the Lenovo ThinkBook Plus (Gen 7) scored 2,388 (Single), 11,445 (Multi), and 22,981 (GPU) in Geekbench 7, and 468 (Single) and 2,559 (Multi) in Cinebench 2026. Those are respectable numbers for this hardware, and Lenovo's thermal system does a good job keeping the Auto Twist cool under load with reasonably quiet fan noise. Two additional cores over something like the HP OmniBook 5 14 (2026) I reviewed definitely make a difference, and the Auto Twist's 4-core GPU is capable of casual gaming, hitting 48FPS in Forza Horizon 6 at 1200p, on Low, and with Intel XeSS enabled. It may not be impressive at this price point, but I'm not disappointed by this laptop's overall performance. With a beefy 75Wh battery and impressive 100W USB-C charging, the ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist has more promising on-paper endurance than performance, and it can deliver a consistent 9–12 hours of real-world usage... as long as you're not using its unique display features. Turning on facial tracking, using voice commands, and otherwise engaging the motorized display takes an alarming chunk out of the Auto Twist's battery, cutting down expected life by as much as 4–6 hours in my testing. That's not altogether unexpected, but it is yet another compromise you must accept if you want a laptop with a 2-axis motorized display. If you are that person, though, I have to ask: who are you? Should you buy the Lenovo ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist? You should buy the ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist if: - You're willing to pay extra for a quirky laptop no one else has. - You can see yourself regularly using the unique display features. - You love being on the experimental side of technology. You should not buy the ThinkBook Plus Auto Twist if: - You want the best performance bang for your buck. - You need guaranteed durability for years to come. - You don't see the point of the motorized display. When I review a product, I ask myself who the product is for, and how well the product fulfills its role for that person. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 was lambasted in my review because — despite generally fantastic hardware — Googlebook OS utterly fails to fulfill its role for the people at whom Googlebooks are aimed. For the Lenovo ThinkBook Plus 14 (Gen 7) Auto Twist, there are plenty of hiccups with the execution, but the greater concern is that it's difficult to even pinpoint who is meant to buy a laptop with a motorized display that can rotate to follow you. Previous ThinkBook Plus ideas had more merit. A secondary E-Ink display is perfect for habitual note-takers; a rollable display is a dream come true for hardcore multitaskers. The situations where you may want the Auto Twist are few, far between, and nebulous enough that the various compromises that come with this display are nearly impossible to swallow. That's before you consider that — like all previous ThinkBook Plus experiments — there may never be a second-generation Auto Twist to address hardware flaws, nor is Lenovo likely to invest in post-launch firmware and software updates to fix issues and add new features. All that to say... I love that this exists. I love that you can actually buy it. I love that Lenovo is experimenting with the decades-old laptop form factor so openly. I even love plenty of things about this laptop — it's incredibly cool. I just can't recommend that you actually buy it unless you're at least as nerdy as I am (and likely far more wealthy).

item.title: REVIEW: Xiaomi’s clip earbuds are so pretty, my social circle confused them for new piercings
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
I’ve tried a bunch of open-ear earbuds over the last couple of years. While I don’t personally gravitate towards them, they serve a few specific and useful features. The freedom they offer has its perks, but they aren’t always comfortable–at least for me. Some have bulky hooks that wrap around your ears, while others start becoming uncomfortable after a few hours. So after Xiaomi sent over the new Clip earbuds, along with the Xiaomi 18 Pros, I was really looking forward to how different these feel, and not just how they sound. After all, clip-on earbuds have become pretty popular, and several manufacturers have already experimented with more fashionable designs. And getting the shiny Sand Gold variant, I wasn’t expecting people to start asking whether I got my ears pierced. Xiaomi’s latest earbuds added a bit of bling to each of my fits, appearing like an elaborate piece of jewelry. This is just one of the reasons why it might be one of my favorite open-ear designs in recent memory. Let’s talk about the design first, because Xiaomi clearly wasn’t trying to be subtle with the Sand Gold finish. The earbuds have a polished metallic appearance, with a polished gold-colored bridge connecting two rounded sections that sit on opposite sides of the ear. Pair this with the speaker housing having a partially transparent design and some circular detailing, and the Xiaomi Clip drops a striking visual combo. The entire thing resembles an oversized ear cuff, and I’ve come to appreciate how much it stands out. Xiaomi also offers more understated finishes, including Graphite Black, Pearl White, and Frost Purple, but the Sand Gold has grown on me quite a bit. But that is just my opinion, and I can imagine the bling not being as appealing to everyone. Some people prefer their earbuds to blend into the background, and there’s absolutely nothing discreet about wearing a shiny gold accessory around your ear. But I appreciate that Xiaomi has embraced the appearance instead of trying to disguise it. In fact, the jewelry resemblance extends beyond the design. When Xiaomi was shipping the earbuds to me, customs actually stopped the package because they suspected it contained some kind of jewelry. I had to explain that the shiny little accessories inside were just Bluetooth earbuds. The whole situation was more amusing than annoying, and I understand why people started asking me about my supposed new piercing. Even the charging case follows a similar design philosophy. Xiaomi has given it a compact, rounded shape with a soft vegan-leather finish, creating something that looks more like a miniature jewelry box than a typical earbud case. As much as I like the passive noise cancellation on typical in-ear earbuds, a sore ear canal after a few hours has always been annoying. One of the great things about open-ear options is their design, but comfort isn’t always guaranteed. I’ve tried several open-ear designs that rely on hooks or flexible loops wrapping around the ear. They fit snugly on your ear, though, prolonged use adds some uncomfortable pressure around the cartilage or behind the ear. Xiaomi Clip doesn’t suffer from this problem. Each earbud weighs just 5.5 grams and uses a relatively rigid titanium memory-wire bridge that clips around the ear. The two rounded sections distribute pressure across the contact points, while the bridge keeps everything securely positioned. I found that the firmer bridge actually helped it be more comfortable overall, and even kept the speaker earpiece in the right position more often. After securing the earbuds, the consistent position keeps the audio more level, as the sound is directed where it needs to go. Xiaomi has also designed the sound outlet to direct audio toward the ear canal, with additional technology intended to reduce sound leakage. Xiaomi has packed these tiny accessories with a lot of tech. The Clip is equipped with 11mm dynamic drivers and support for the LHDC 5.0 high-resolution audio codec. The company also promises up to nine hours of playback on a single charge, extending to 38 hours with the charging case. However, I’m saving a more detailed assessment of sound quality, microphone performance, and battery endurance for another time. But the best part is definitely how naturally these earbuds feel when I’m wearing them. I’ve always appreciated technology that manages to bring a little personality to everyday gadgets. Xiaomi has done exactly that with the Clip–turning something as ordinary as wireless earbuds into an accessory people actually notice. The Sand Gold finish is unapologetically flashy, and I’m sure some people would rather have something far more understated. Personally, I’ve enjoyed every moment of wearing them.

item.title: REVIEW: ‘Punch Punch Forever!’ Is a Gem
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
Independent animation projects on YouTube are having a moment, and I’m loving every second of it. But if I had to pick my absolute favorite show from the treasure trove of series out now, it’d be Punch Punch Forever! Created by YouTube animator Speedoru in 2023, Punch Punch Forever! is a delightfully anachronistic independent web-animated series with the look and soul of a ’90s Saturday morning shonen anime discovered on a dusty VHS tape. It follows Gogo, a powerful, bespectacled little girl with gag-manga levels of strength akin to Goku from OG Dragon Ball, living in a world where humans and demons kinda sorta co-exist. In keeping with the Dragon Ball-ness of the series, the only thing that seems to keep this fraught society in check is its world’s version of the Budokai Tenkaichi tournament, a martial arts competition where the victor gets their wish granted. Only instead of the wish-granter being a giant, sprawling green dragon, it’s the wide-chested Emperor Koro. What follows is grade-A anime “qualityslop,” where Gogo slimes out fearsome foes all while her doting mother, sardonic half-demon sister, and cool pet frog cheer her on from the sidelines. It’s a “What did I just watch, and why do I want to watch more of it?” kinda show, and I hope more people will join me in loving it to death. Though, I don’t think it needs my word-of-mouth recommendation, since its pilot episode has over 7.6 million views, and its fourth episode has already amassed over 1.4 million views despite being only two days old at the time of writing. The best way I can describe Punch Punch Forever! is as a pastiche of a Saturday morning anime block, with a sprinkle of beat-’em-up mayhem à la River City Girls and a touch of Smiling Friends-style humor. As someone who grew up in the halcyon days of YouTube, when parody animation projects were thriving long before influencers and drama channels took over, what I love most about Punch Punch Forever! is the sheer amount of effort on display in every frame. Rather than merely poke fun at anime, the series celebrates it through its own brand of slapstick storytelling. The jokes land, too. Its bits have me laughing just as hard as Smiling Friends once did. Punch Punch Forever! has a little something for everyone. It’s packed with gnarly, hyper-detailed close-ups that evoke SpongeBob SquarePants at its most grotesque, Ranma 1/2-style martial arts hijinks, and faces chiseled straight out of Fist of the North Star. The result is a have-your-cake-and-eat-it-too anime parody, loaded with all the genre’s defining hallmarks: an earworm opening theme, eye-catching commercial bumpers featuring artwork from different artists rendered in a vaporwave style, and the occasional fourth-wall break. Beyond its Dragon Ball anime allure, Punch Punch Forever! also features episodes parodying Friday the 13th, competitive obstacle-course challenges like Sasuke (American Ninja Warrior), and even its own Christmas special. Between the static-laced faux commercials and random snippets of live-action Japanese television, you can practically hear an aging VCR buzz every time the image flickers across the screen. In addition to its anime lampooning, Punch Punch Forever! occasionally dips into visual gags that recall the era when sitcoms like Martin and The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air would toss an obvious mannequin across the set to sell the impact of someone getting absolutely walloped. My absolute favorite episode of Punch Punch Forever! is the third, “Toothless Aggression.” As a fan of the graps and anime, this episode feels like Speedoru molded an Amigara Fault especially for me. Alongside Gogo’s usual Tenkaichi tournament shenanigans, this episode has her duke it out against professional wrestler send-ups to WWE’s Mega Powers, which consisted of Hulk Hogan and Macho Man Randy Savage. This time, Gogo isn’t battling alone. We get to see her mom enter the ring, tornado tag team style. But what really sells the episode for me is how Speedoru somehow got potty-mouthed Stardom wrestler/idol Maki Itoh to voice act an equally spitfire wrestling manager in the show. And for the anime holdouts among us still fighting the dubs vs subs war despite it being old hat, the animated series’ whole anime-ness is that it recently received an English dub compilation on YouTube that’s just as madcap and sidesplittingly hilarious as its Japanese dub. Forget streaming. The best ’90s anime throwback that captures retro magic in a contemporary package is Punch Punch Forever! Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: SALES: Best Thunderbolt docks to extend your laptop’s capabilities
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
A Thunderbolt laptop docking station offers a serious boost to your productivity, providing support for old and new peripherals alike. It’s a necessity for a home office, but only buy what you need: In 2026, premium Thunderbolt 5 docks might be overkill for a Windows PC. Here, we’ll recommend the best Thunderbolt docks — an overall pick, as well as budget and premium recommendations — based on our own testing of dozens of Thunderbolt docking stations. That testing includes a formal performance evaluation, of course, but also simply using each dock day-in and day-out over an extended period. If you need help deciding what’s best for you, a FAQ at the bottom of the page is there to assist. That FAQ includes an explanation of why I generally lean toward slightly older Thunderbolt 4 docks at the moment. Be aware that significantly older laptops often don’t use Thunderbolt. They may have a slower, generic USB-C port instead, making my picks for the best USB-C hubs and dongles a better choice. If you have a Ryzen laptop, you’re rocking USB4 instead of Thunderbolt 4, although the two are essentially interchangeable. If you’re interested in productivity and not gaming, consider a middle ground: my favorite DisplayLink USB-C docks. I explain how to make that decision below these recommendations. Why you should trust PCWorld for Thunderbolt dock reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been in business since the late 1980s, featuring a steady stream of news, reviews, how-to articles, and more. We don’t try to cover every topic under the sun. Instead, we focus on what you need to know — and buy — in the world of PCs. I’ve been personally reviewing these docks for several years now. Kensington Thunderbolt 4 Dual 4K Dock (SD5780T) – Best overall Thunderbolt dock - Pretty solid mix of ports, including downstream Thunderbolt 4 - Price cuts have helped make it more affordable - One display port, requiring an additional dongle for two displays - No dedicated phone charging port, but Thunderbolt can do it Who should buy the Kensington SD5780T? The SD5780T is an ideal “starter” dock, for someone who has a laptop and a single external display and might want to add more in the future. Adding a second display will require the purchase of a USB-C (Thunderbolt) to HDMI cable, which will cost an additional $15 or so. The inclusion of the SD card slot should appeal to photographers who record photo or video on those cards. One of my testing credos is “affordable flexibility,” and I favor a dock that will fit into your existing setup. But I also don’t want you to pay through the nose for it. Still, even the cost of the additional cable isn’t much, and this dock’s price is right where I’d hope it to be, about $250 or so. (It’s also why we include a range of retailers: When I updated this in February 2026, Lenovo was selling this dock for $50 less than other sites.) Kensington SD5780T: Further considerations The Kensington SD5780T is a solid Thunderbolt 4 dock in all respects. For those who wish to use a single 4K monitor, chances are that you already own an HDMI cable. In my tests, the dock was stable (and not all are!) with a nice port selection. The dock will charge your smartphone if you connect its USB-C charging cable to the Thunderbolt port. The bottom line: This is currently among the best combination of value and features in a Thunderbolt dock that I’ve tested. - Four display ports that eliminate extra cables - Four simultaneous 4K display outputs are possible only in some scenarios This is a good choice for a multi-monitor user who doesn’t want to have to think about adapter cables. This dock includes both HDMI as well as DisplayPort connections, and, depending on the capabilities of your PC, you can connect up to four displays. This makes this dock ideal for a desktop PC or for a “battlestation” of multiple displays. If it wasn’t for the iffy charging capabilities, this might be our top dock right now. Normally, docks that include a ton of ports cost a lot more — and this StarTech dock did too. But for right now, Amazon is charging about $204 for this dock on discount, which is insanely good. Price absolutely matters to my recommendations, so be sure and buy it if the price holds to that point. Otherwise, keep in mind that this dock doesn’t offer the peripheral power that some others do, and its single USB-C port might not be satisfactory to some buyers — that’s what our primary pick above is for. Wavlink Thunderbolt 4 Triple Display Docking Station – Best budget Thunderbolt dock - Two ports for fast-charging smartphones Who should buy the Wavlink Thunderbolt 4 Triple Display Docking Station? Like the StarTech above, this is a dock for you if multiple external displays matter more than compactness. This affordable yet capable Thunderbolt 4 dock offers a generous set of extra ports and the ability to connect a couple of 4K displays. Wavlink Thunderbolt 4 Triple Display Docking Station: Further considerations For this I’m leaning on Macworld’s choice of docks, which offers an excellent feature set at an affordable price — and it will work just fine with Windows machines. The dock is a well-priced and loaded Thunderbolt 4 dock, though it sacrifices two of the potential three downstream TB4 ports in favor of two HDMI 2.1 ports. Use one of these for one external display and the downstream TB4 port for the other. The spare HDMI port can be used for a third extended display on Windows PCs. Power delivery to the laptop is 96W, enough for a lightweight content-creation laptop. There’s a handy 30W USB-C charging port at the front, which also supports 10Gbps data transfer. Note that’s not enough to fast-charge the very latest smartphones, but is satisfactory for older models. Ugreen Revodok Pro 13-in-1 Triple Display Docking Station – Best budget Thunderbolt dock runner-up - You’ll need your own power supply/charger Who should buy the Ugreen Revodok Pro 13-in-1 Triple Display Docking Station? I recommend this dock for those who own laptops with 13th-gen Core hardware or above. HBR3/DSC technology really doesn’t work on older systems like 11th-gen Core hardware and older PCs. If you own an AMD Ryzen laptop, too, it may be a little iffy. Great price, though! Ugreen Revodok Pro 13-in-1 Triple Display Docking Station: Further considerations The only reason this isn’t my pick for the best budget Thunderbolt docking station is because it uses a generic form of data compression known as HBR3 (High Bit Rate 3) with DSC (Display Stream Compression), which is built into the DisplayPort spec. That’s a particular technology that is more common within recent Intel Core (and Core Ultra) laptops, but isn’t guaranteed to appear on yours. (If you own a laptop with a Thunderbolt port, though, this should work just fine.) You’ll also have to supply your own USB-C power cable. Otherwise, this docking station has so much to offer. The price is outstanding, of course, but Ugreen’s dock is also so flexible yet so stable. Everything’s well labeled, and the dock offers DisplayPort as well as HDMI options. And it’s really quite portable, too. Just remember that charger. Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 SSD Dock – Best premium Thunderbolt dock - Higher SSD capacities quickly elevate the price Who should buy the Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 SSD Dock? Yes, this is the same dock I selected as my overall pick. But if you’re looking for a premium Thunderbolt dock, I think this fits the bill. We have a cheaper runner-up option just below. Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 SSD Dock: Further considerations The performance that this dock offers really boils down to the integrated SSD. It’s simply one of the fastest storage options that I’ve tested for an external drive, though it’s confined to the dock. (It’s not removeable.) But if you want a 4GB SSD option, you’ll pay $750 (at press time). That’s kind of insane. Kensington SD7100T5 EQ Pro 19-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station – Best premium Thunderbolt dock runner-up - Dock will charge without need for a laptop connection - Unusually varied ports (optical, CompactFlash) - Some trouble connecting to displays after a restart/resume Who should buy the Kensington SD7100T5 EQ Pro 19-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station? This dock is definitely for the prosumer, or someone with some extra spending cash. This dock has it all: M.2 slot. Hot keys. An optical connection. Offline charging. CompactFlash. If you’re a high-end creative professional, you should be reading the linked review below with one hand on your wallet. Kensington SD7100T5 EQ Pro 19-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 Docking Station: Further considerations I absolutely think that this is more dock than the average person will need, especially in a year where Thunderbolt 5 isn’t a necessity. But there’s enough here for professionals today, especially with an eye toward the future. But man, what a price tag! I would hope and expect that Kensington lowers the price during 2026. Plugable 5-in-1 Thunderbolt Hub (USB4-HUB3A) – Best Thunderbolt 4 hub - 15W/60W of charging power to phones/PCs - Best for Thunderbolt-attached displays Who should buy the Plugable 5-in-1 Thunderbolt Hub (USB4-HUB3A)? First, you want to understand the difference between a dock and a hub. Primarily it’s in the number and variety of ports, with hubs being smaller and extending the selection of USB-C ports. This hub is a good choice for users of Thunderbolt/USB-C monitors, which are much more common in the Mac market but may become more prevalent in the Windows space in the future. A USB-C monitor tends to also have legacy ports (USB-A, USB-C) inside them, which means that a Thunderbolt dock and its cluster of ports may be redundant. This hub is a way to save a little money for the user who has a specific setup. Plugable 5-in-1 Thunderbolt Hub (USB4-HUB3A): Further considerations With this hub there’s less of an emphasis on legacy ports, and more of a focus on a direct connection to a display. Also, this thing is tiny (4.75 x 2.88 x 0.5 inches) even if, unfortunately, the associated power brick isn’t. It will send 15W of power via the Thunderbolt/USB-C connections to charge smartphones, and 60W to the host PC. If you don’t need a big, bulky dock with multiple connections, Plugable’s 5-in-1 Hub just does the job and without any extra fuss. If your laptop needs more power than the 60W Plugable hub provides, I would recommend the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Slim Hub Pro instead. Razer Thunderbolt 4 Dock Chroma – Best Thunderbolt 4 hub runner-up - A higher price tag than what rivals charge Who should buy the Razer Thunderbolt 4 Dock Chroma? Gamers, obviously. But even a stodgy old reporter like me likes it, because the RGB can either be fixed to a certain color or turned off entirely. And the dock surprised me with its stability and construction. You can certainly buy this dock for its blingy aesthetic, but it works just as well as a more down-to-earth alternative, too. Razer did a very nice job balancing both aspects. Razer Thunderbolt 4 Dock Chroma: Further considerations I was surprised by how much I like this combination dock/hub. It’s a premium offering, with enough ports that I’d almost consider it a full-fledged dock. But with three upstream Thunderbolt ports, you can characterize it as a hub as well. As one of the more modern docks, with rock-solid stability, it won me over in the end, though its storage performance was middling. And, of course, remember to invest in cables. The RGB lighting is fun, and optional — it can be turned off. Plugable USB4 Dual HDMI Docking Station (UD-4VPD) – Best USB4 docking station - 4K120 display capabilities open up gaming possibilities - Storage tests across the dock were lower than average Who should buy the Plugable USB4 Dual HDMI Docking Station (UD-4VPD)? This is a general-purpose USB4 dock, which can be adopted by anyone. But it’s best suited for laptops with a Ryzen chip inside, and for photographers who need the SD card slots. Plugable USB4 Dual HDMI Docking Station (UD-4VPD): Further considerations Thunderbolt and USB4 are basically the same. USB4 ports typically appear on laptops with AMD Ryzen chips inside (because Intel refuses to certify an AMD laptop as Thunderbolt-compliant.) Why include a dedicated USB4 category? In part, because not everyone knows this. This dock can get hot, but it’s an affordable budget option. CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock – Best Thunderbolt dock for Apple Mac users - 15 top-end ports, including four Thunderbolt 5 Who should buy the CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock? This is the dock for hardcore Mac users, according to our colleagues at Macworld. Right now, Thunderbolt 5 docks are more suited to Macs, with their higher-resolution displays. The CalDigit TS5 Plus has just about everything you need—indeed probably more than you need. The plain TS5’s 15 ports should be enough for any but the more extreme pro-level users, Macworld says, as part of its list of the best Thunderbolt docking stations for the Apple Mac. CalDigit TS5 Thunderbolt 5 Dock: Further considerations The TS5 actually offers one more downstream Thunderbolt 5 port than the CalDigit TS5 Plus, which sacrificed one of its TB5 ports for a DisplayPort. On the other hand, high-end Mac displays include a dedicated Thunderbolt or USB-C connection. If you need to connect high-performance SSDs or RAID devices Thunderbolt 5 rewards you with a PCIe 4.0 performance at 64Gbps, and the dock supports transfer speeds up to 6,200MBps. But yikes! $400 is a lot, even for a high-end dock. MacBook buyers: Pay for Thunderbolt 5 only if your display or storage workflow can use it. DisplayLink USB-C docks, which I discuss in more detail in a separate article, don’t offer enough bandwidth for high-refresh rate monitors or gaming, but they work admirably well for everyday office work, including watching movies. Anecdotally, they’ve often been more stable than a Thunderbolt dock on older hardware, as sometimes Thunderbolt docks have issues “waking up” when the host laptop wakes up from standby. You can “break” the dock by pushing more and more over the connection, like streaming while copying files. What I’d like to see in a DisplayLink USB-C docking station is a feature set that approaches a full-fledged Thunderbolt dock, but that is priced below what you’d pay for Thunderbolt performance. The current pick does just that. Some recent reviews do not appear here — for instance, StarTech’s USB-C Triple Monitor Dock fell short. Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615 – Best USB-C DisplayLink dock - Can warm to somewhat alarming temperatures Who should buy the Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615? If you’re not worried about hunting down the proper software driver (because Ugreen, bless them, does not make it apparent that it needs one) than I would recommend that you buy this dock. It offers many of the features of more expensive Thunderbolt docks at an affordable price. Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615: Further considerations Like some of our premium Thunderbolt docks, Ugreen provides options to use either HDMI or DisplayPort to connect a display, allowing you to use your existing display cables and save some money. Like most DisplayLink docks, this dock was unusually stable, with no flickering between displays — one of the reasons I like DisplayLink docks. Some other Thunderbolt docks offer the same flexibility to shift between monitors, but not many. Ugreen’s dock does so affordably. Plugable USB-C Dual 4K Display Horizontal Docking Station (UD-6950PDH) – Best USB-C DisplayLink dock runner-up Who should buy the Plugable USB-C Dual 4K Display Horizontal Docking Station? If you’re a home office worker who doesn’t want or need to game, this dock will suit you just fine. Plugable’s USB-C Dual 4K Display dock takes Plugable’s traditional approach: Provide dedicated display interfaces, and let the user choose between which cables they’ll need to connect to their display. The dock is a pretty simple affair, with a pair of legacy USB-A ports and standard gigabit Ethernet connection. Interestingly, Plugable has recast this dock as a Mac-dedicated device, with a grayish tint to boot. (That’s what you’ll see on the Amazon page.) It’s really not — it will work on Macs and Windows PCs just fine, though you’ll need the Windows driver for it instead. Plugable USB-C Dual 4K Display Horizontal Docking Station: Further considerations For whatever reason (maybe the bandwidth that a 10Gbps port consumes?) USB-C ports aren’t common on DisplayLink docks. (The Ugreen dock that we’ve picked as our favorite has one; this dock does not.) This is going to sound redundant, but just keep in mind that these docks are terrific for video playback or office work, but gaming is beyond them. - StarTech.com Thunderbolt 4/USB4 Quad Display Docking Station: A recent price cut makes this dock a top buy. Check it out. - OWC ships the first two-meter Thunderbolt 5 cable. One-meter cables can be a tad short. OWC’s active cable adds extra flexibility. - Razer Thunderbolt 5 Dock Chroma review: Too many things went wrong here for me to recommend this dock. - Wavlink Thunderbolt 4 Dock (UTD45): I disagree with our sister site, Macworld: it’s just not as good as promised. - Plugable TBT-UDT3 Thunderbolt 5 dock review: Plugable makes solid docks, but this one is also moderately priced for a TB5 dock. - Sonnet Echo 13 Thunderbolt 5 SSD Dock: Why it’s the best laptop dock I’ve reviewed - The biggest thing I didn’t see at CES: Thunderbolt 5: Thunderbolt 5 was a no-show, and insiders explain why. - My first Thunderbolt 5 experience was a huge bust: I don’t know whether it was the cable, laptop, or dock, but my first taste of Thunderbolt 5 was a lot worse than I expected. - Is Thunderbolt 5 storage ready? Thunderbolt 5 exhibits a marked improvement in sequential transfers, but our first look at the spec suffered some backwards-compatibility issues. - Kensington’s first Thunderbolt 5 dock is built for the future: Thunderbolt 5 is here…but you’ll need more than just this well-built Kensington docking station to take advantage of it. Can I get a better deal on Thunderbolt docks? Let’s face it: Tariffs have been a major wild card on all sorts of purchases. Daily discounts and so-called “lightning deals” affect prices, too. Thunderbolt docks, however, still receive discounts during major shopping events like Amazon’s Prime Day deals and holiday sales. While our automated pricing technology that we use in our reviews should reflect the current price of the item, it’s always a good idea to check PCWorld’s list of deals for these major shopping events. We generally dedicate specific articles to the best deals on Thunderbolt docks and USB-C hubs. I’ve written a separate article about how I test Thunderbolt docks, which goes into detail about how evaluate the performance of docks. Put very briefly, I examine each dock physically, making measurements on the cord length and port spacing. I then connect the dock to a variety of laptops. My performance testing includes streaming video, transferring video files back and forth, running standardized benchmarks, and more. In addition, I simply use the dock for several days just to discover any quirks or glitches. Who curated this article? My name is Mark Hachman, and I’ve covered the technology industry as a reporter and reviewer for over 30 years. I’ve worked from home for years, so when the pandemic hit I instantly realized that all the things I had already nerded out about — using a laptop docking station, setting up multiple monitors — would become a priority for PCWorld’s readers. When someone tells me that they bought one of the docking stations that I’ve recommended, and that they love it — well, that’s why I do what I do. Ports, cables, peripherals: Those are the three major considerations when buying a Thunderbolt dock. Check your laptop’s specifications. As a general rule, a dock from the Thunderbolt 4 family is the default buy for most people. It will work with laptops with a Thunderbolt 5 connection, but at Thunderbolt 4 speeds. Still, you may save a few bucks with an older dock. Thunderbolt 5, if your laptop supports it, is the better choice if you expect to run high-end storage or display setups. Think about what you want to connect the dock to. Here, the priority is usually the displays. Consider the displays you own (which typically include either HDMI or DisplayPort connections) and think about whether the dock will accommodate them. I prefer docks with dedicated display ports, so that a display with an HDMI port, for example, can connect directly. I am seeing a small but growing percentage of Thunderbolt docks that include a Thunderbolt cable to your laptop and then dedicated Thunderbolt connections out to displays. These docks tend to cater to Mac users. However, you can buy a dongle or cable that converts Thunderbolt/ USB-C to HDMI or DisplayPort, or else you can buy a USB-C display. What will you want to plug into the dock? Use that answer as a guide. Do you want a basic Thunderbolt dock, with just a pair of HDMI ports for connecting two displays? Does an SD card slot matter? How many USB Type A peripherals do you plan to attach? Do you want to charge your smartphone? More recent phones now require more power to fast-charge them. Check your laptop’s power supply. Does it plug into your laptop via USB-C? If so, a Thunderbolt dock will likely power it. You’ll need to understand how the dock supplies power, though. Check your laptop’s charger to learn how much power it supplies, and how much the dock will need to supply to replace it. If your laptop or devices aren’t receiving enough power, you may see a warning pop up. A “bus-powered” dock won’t come with an external charger in the package, saving some cost, space, and power concerns. (Today, these are pretty rare.) A dock with power delivery will supply its own power and charge your laptop and/or a phone via your laptop’s existing USB-C charger. What I’ve found is that some docks, especially those with a free Thunderbolt port, will supply enough power for even today’s most modern fast-charging smartphones, even without explicit support for them. There’s one more consideration: the length of the Thunderbolt cable between your laptop and the dock itself. You may have noticed or heard about USB-C ports wearing out on smartphones; a loose or wobbly connector on a Thunderbolt dock can cause a monitor to unexpectedly flicker or lose connection. Consider how much tension will be put on a cable. A Thunderbolt dock that’s dangling from a Thunderbolt port will stress the physical connector. You don’t want that! We’re starting to see some docks with an SSD enclosure inside. It’s possible that this will become more of a viable product over time, but for now it’s still niche. If you’re a Mac user who has stumbled across this article, welcome. But please be aware that early Apple MacBook Pros powered by Intel silicon supported up to two 4K displays. The first MacBook Pros powered by the Apple M1 chip only support a single 4K display. Many Mac users have recently left negative reviews on Thunderbolt docks on shopping sites because of this. Apple also hasn’t explicitly committed to Thunderbolt 5, either. Buy a PC! How do I know if my laptop has Thunderbolt? The short answer: Look at the laptop’s published specifications to be sure. A Thunderbolt port uses a USB-C connection, and it may look indistinguishable from a USB-C port. Put another way: All Thunderbolt ports are USB-C, but not all USB-C ports are Thunderbolt-equipped. Thunderbolt ports are supposed to have a small lightning-bolt icon to identify them. But some laptop makers use a similar lightning-bolt icon to indicate that a USB-C port can be used for charging your phone, and not for Thunderbolt. Laptop makers sometimes don’t want to clutter the clean lines of their products by adding additional logos, it seems. Fortunately, most laptops now choose to highlight their Thunderbolt capabilities, so the ports should be well-marked. In June 2024, Intel held a technical session talking about its Core Ultra 200 (Lunar Lake) processor. One of the big changes Intel said it would make was to force laptop makers to a) cluster all of the older USB-C ports on one side of the laptop, away from the Thunderbolt and b) require the ports (including Thunderbolt) to be clearly labeled. That didn’t happen. USB4 is Thunderbolt’s more generic competitor, and USB4 docks and Thunderbolt docks are often interchangeable. The USB Implementor’s Forum is going to ask laptop makers to add a separate, different USB4 logo to laptops as well. This strikes me as unnecessarily confusing. How fast is Thunderbolt? Put simply, 40Gbps, for Thunderbolt 3 or 4. Most USB-C ports are built on the second-generation USB 3.1 data-transfer standard, which transfers data at 10Gbps. Thunderbolt 3 and 4 ports, the most common standard, transfer data at up to 40Gbps. Thunderbolt 4 differs very slightly in that it supports a theoretical maximum of 32Gbps for external storage devices, but you probably won’t notice the difference. Intel unveiled an 80Gbps version of Thunderbolt in 2024, called Thunderbolt 5, meaning that you’ll see Thunderbolt docks with even more capabilities. In certain scenarios, Thunderbolt 5 can reroute data to deliver 120Gbps in one direction. More laptops are arriving with a discrete Thunderbolt 5 chip inside, though they’re still somewhat rare and tend to land inside gaming laptops. What should I buy: Thunderbolt 3, Thunderbolt 4, or Thunderbolt 5? It’s not a bad idea to match your laptop’s hardware specification to the dock: Thunderbolt 3 to Thunderbolt 3, Thunderbolt 4 to Thunderbolt 4, and so on. Thunderbolt 3 and 4 are basically the same, though retailers have almost entirely phased out their Thunderbolt 3 dock inventory. The default choice is a Thunderbolt 4 dock. You can always future-proof your setup with an 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 laptop and dock. but those aren’t essential quite yet. I would normally say that Thunderbolt 5 docks are backwards-compatible to Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 3 docks, but that doesn’t seem always true. If you own a laptop with a Thunderbolt 3 port, do not buy a Thunderbolt 5 dock; chances are that it won’t work. Please be aware that, early in 2026, only a few Apple Macs include dedicated Thunderbolt 5 ports, alongside a scattering of Windows gaming laptops. Neither Intel nor AMD support Thunderbolt 5 on their 2026 laptop platforms, meaning that laptop makers have to buy a separate chip. For that reason, Thunderbolt 5 makes sense if you anticipate a future where Intel’s gaming laptops or future platforms natively support Thunderbolt 5. Otherwise, Thunderbolt 5 is best for Macs. Here’s the long answer to the question asked above: Essentially, Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4 allow up to 40Gbps maximum bandwidth, enough for two 4K/60 displays. “Up to” is the key phrase: Thunderbolt 3 is only required to support a 10Gbps connection, allowing for a single external 4K display (a 16Gbps PCIe connection, paired with USB 3.2). Most manufacturers go beyond this, however, and our recommended docks support the full 40Gbps specification (and two 4K displays) unless noted. Thunderbolt 3 also supports a slower (16Gbps) PCIe connection for connecting to external storage. Thunderbolt 3 is also the only specification (not Thunderbolt 4) that we’ve seen connecting to external GPUs, in case you’d like to try that approach. Thunderbolt 5 adds that capability back, but few docks take advantage of it. Thunderbolt 3 was somewhat flexible from a standards perspective. Thunderbolt 4 doesn’t allow for any leeway—you’re getting a full-fledged 40Gbps connection (32Gbps PCIe + USB 3.2), no questions asked. For external storage, Thunderbolt 4 supports 32Gbps of data transfer—this really only matters for video, external GPU connections, or possibly games. Thunderbolt 4 supports “wake on sleep” from an external keyboard or mouse, which allows you to tap your external keyboard or wiggle your mouse to wake up your PC, which is handy. Thunderbolt 4 allows for longer cables and more Thunderbolt ports on laptops, too. Device maker Anker has a nice table of all of the technical features associated with Thunderbolt 3, Thunderbolt 4, and USB4, if you really want to get into the fine distinctions (below). What’s USB4? We address that further down. I already own a USB-C dongle. Can I use it with Thunderbolt? Yes, you can connect the dongle to a Thunderbolt port. But the 10Gbps dongle won’t magically transform into a 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, as there’s circuitry within the dock that allows it to work with your laptop’s high-speed Thunderbolt port. However, there’s nothing saying that you can’t connect the dongle to an available USB-C port on the Thunderbolt dock itself, either. If your laptop has two Thunderbolt ports, you can also attach a Thunderbolt dock to one port, and the dongle to the other. That solution will add more clutter to your desk, but it might allow you to buy a cheaper, budget dock, too. It’s up to you! My laptop says it has a USB4 port, not Thunderbolt. Can I use it with a Thunderbolt dock? Probably. USB4 ports typically appear on laptops with AMD Ryzen processors inside. USB4 and Thunderbolt 4 are compatible and functionally equivalent. (Though Thunderbolt is an open standard, Intel declines to certify non-Intel hardware. That means that Ryzen laptops end up with USB4 ports, and Intel Core laptops include Thunderbolt.) As a subset of Thunderbolt 4, a USB4 device will run just fine plugged into a Thunderbolt 4 port. But dock makers tell us that a Thunderbolt 4 device may not work as expected when plugged into what is specifically a USB4 port. Instead, most hubs and docks are marketed as Thunderbolt 4, while most devices (like an external SSD) are designed around USB4. (We test Thunderbolt docks on Thunderbolt laptops.) There are USB4 docks, however, which you’ll find above in our list of best picks. USB4 Version 2 is a standard that will propel USB4 to 80Gbps, just like Thunderbolt 5. I haven’t seen any docking stations marketed as USB v2 (also known as USB80Gbps), however. Note that Thunderbolt 3 and 4 require at least 15W to power devices plugged into the Thunderbolt port, such as a bus-powered hard drive. USB4 requires just half that. I did try to connect a Thunderbolt 5 dock to a USB4 laptop, and it didn’t work. It should! It may just be a driver issue. What is so important about Thunderbolt 5? The Thunderbolt 5 spec pushes I/O bandwidth from 40Gbps in Thunderbolt 4 to 80Gbps in Thunderbolt 5, and even to 120Gbps in some cases. Another good way to think of Thunderbolt 5 is in the context of what it can do. Thunderbolt 4 allows enough bandwidth for two 4K displays, running at 60Hz. Thunderbolt 5 will offer enough bandwidth to connect to three 4K displays, at 144Hz apiece. That helps make Thunderbolt 5 a gaming-class technology, rather than just for office work. Thunderbolt 5 will also allow for 64Gbps of dedicated bandwidth for storage and external GPUs, double the 32Gbps on Thunderbolt 4. Finally, there’s power. Thunderbolt 5 will provide up to 240W (140W required) of charging power for your laptop. Most laptops require 65W to 90W today, but gaming laptops require more. All this means is that a Thunderbolt 5 dock will potentially eliminate the need to carry a gaming laptop’s charger around. (It won’t be in all cases, but some.) Note that you’ll need a laptop that supports this power spec, however! And that’s the problem. Thunderbolt 5 debuted in 2024, both in laptops as well as docks and devices. Although we saw a couple of early products in 2024, I only saw two TB5 laptops for several months: a version of the Razer Blade and the Maingear ML-17. Both have discrete chips inside, rather than being directly integrated inside the processor. I tried a Thunderbolt 5 setup, and it stunk, though I think it’s the fault of Maingear’s laptop, and not the docks. Why does that matter? If a function like Thunderbolt 5 isn’t built right into the processor, a laptop OEM must buy it separately. That takes time, money, and engineering, and most laptop makers think hard before spending extra. There are a few Thunderbolt 5 docks, but hardly any laptops that support it. At CES 2025, I was told that it may take a couple of years for Thunderbolt 5 to really go mainstream — 2026 or maybe 2027. In 2026, that seems likely to be the case. Thunderbolt 5 isn’t integrated into Intel’s Lunar Lake mobile processor, and it’s not in the desktop or mobile versions of Arrow Lake, either. Maybe Panther Lake? Nope. Thunderbolt Share is a new way of connecting two PCs via a Thunderbolt cable. Plug one end of the cable into one Thunderbolt port, and the other into a Thunderbolt port on another laptop, and voila! They’re connected. Thunderbolt Share allows you to use one PC to control another, sync files, share files, and more, all at Thunderbolt speeds. I explain Thunderbolt Share and test it, here. It sounds simple, easy, and powerful, but it’s more complicated than that. Both PCs have to run Intel’s Thunderbolt Share software, and you’ll only be able to get that from a licensed PC or Thunderbolt dock. Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 5 will run Thunderbolt Share, but not Thunderbolt 3 — well, officially. The same goes for USB 4; it might work, and it might not. Intel isn’t saying. Thunderbolt Share will be supported by a handful of PC makers as well as dock makers like Belkin, Plugable, and more. But you know what? That announcement kind of came and went. I’m not betting on Thunderbolt Share being more than a gimmick right now. What cable should I use with a Thunderbolt dock? Virtually every Thunderbolt dock will ship with its own cable. We recommend that you use Thunderbolt 3 cables with Thunderbolt 3 products, and Thunderbolt 4 cables with Thunderbolt 4 products. Ditto for the first Thunderbolt 5 cables, when the technology ships. My Thunderbolt docking station only has Thunderbolt connections, but I need to connect it to my monitor. How can I connect a Thunderbolt dock to my HDMI display? You’ll need a special USB-C to HDMI cable, rated for Thunderbolt speeds. I recommend and have purchased this Uni Thunderbolt to HDMI cable from Amazon, which is about $16. You can find cheaper options, but make sure they’re rated for either Thunderbolt or a 4K@60Hz display. What differentiates a DisplayLink USB-C docking station from a Thunderbolt dock? A DisplayLink USB-C docking station is a new category of docking station. They’re often marketed just as a USB-C docking station, unfortunately, though the DisplayLink logo features prominently on the box. The key here is that the DisplayLink technology (now owned by Synaptics) uses data compression between your PC and the dock to approximate a Thunderbolt experience (a pair of 4K displays at 60Hz, plus additional peripherals) across the narrower, slower USB-C bus. You’ll need to install a software driver for your PC to communicate with the DisplayLink chip built into the dock. The advantage here is twofold. First, DisplayLink allows you to “cheat” and get a Thunderbolt dock experience on an older laptop. Alternatively, even if you do own a laptop with a Thunderbolt port, you may be able to find a DisplayLink USB-C dock for a cheaper price than Thunderbolt. This is a viable solution, especially if you don’t mind not playing PC games. Our separate story on DisplayLink docks has more. For a while, DisplayLink offered a consistently cheaper option than Thunderbolt. Older Thunderbolt technologies and tariffs have now muddled those waters that the distinction isn’t as clear-cut. What is HBR3 with DSC? We’re starting to see some USB-C docking stations take advantage of another technology: HBR3 (High Bit Rate 3) with DSC (Display Stream Compression). Think of it as the industry-standard, manufacturer-agnostic version of DisplayLink. It works over the USB-C port, and again provides a dual 4K60 display experience. The problem? It’s wonky. I’ve found that support for the technology was very iffy in 11th-gen hardware, and really seems to work consistently in 12th-gen or 13th-gen Core laptops (and above, when they ship). It’s becoming more common, however, and works more stably in the most recent Intel Core laptops. At CES 2026, though, I did see the VESA standards body propose a sticker for DSC, to let customers know they have it. Can I use an external graphics card (eGPU) with Thunderbolt? With Thunderbolt 3? Yes, you can. Certain manufacturers (Razer is one, though there are others) have built enclosures that can house a standard desktop graphics card, connected to your laptop via a Thunderbolt cable. Although a mobile gaming laptop with an external GPU does a good job enabling mobile gaming, a desktop GPU does even better. Thunderbolt simply connects the two. External GPU support sort of skipped Thunderbolt 4, however, and I would recommend using a Thunderbolt 3 dock instead, or wait until Thunderbolt 5. How can you hook up an external GPU to your laptop via Thunderbolt? Our story has more. The only eGPUs I’ve seen with Thunderbolt use Thunderbolt 3, not Thunderbolt 4. Why is that? According to a representative for Razer, the differences between Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4 were too small. “When we release any product, we only do so when there can be a material advantage over the previous generation,” we were told. Since Thunderbolt 4 was backwards compatible and functionally equivalent to Thunderbolt 3, Razer simply declined to invest in the production and testing of a Thunderbolt 4 eGPU. I presume other manufacturers followed suit. I want to charge my phone with a Thunderbolt dock. What do I need to know?
