I specifically updated this question in February 2026, with the release of the Samsung Galaxy S26 lineup. These new phones require a full 60W to charge, which no Thunderbolt 4 dock I’ve seen can accomplish. (An iPhone 17 requires 40W.) A Thunderbolt 4 dock can deliver up to 140W to a laptop (known as host charging), but not commonly out through a USB-C charging port. I have also yet to see a Thunderbolt dock with wireless charging built in. Some USB-C docks do have this feature. Still, the S26 can use up to 25W for wireless charging, as can the iPhone 17. This is a shortcoming of these docks, and we’ll have to see if it can be overcome.

By now, the importance of backing up your Windows PC or laptop goes without saying. Just take a moment to consider how much of your data is at potential risk of a drive failure, natural disaster, or a bad actor, if you don’t have a solid backup plan in place. The best Windows backup software includes file backup, sure, but also disk imaging and full image restore, as well as disaster recovery. Our picks for best Windows backup software are selected with all the must-haves of data backup and recovery in mind, so in the tragic event that your primary local data repository is compromised, you’re fully covered. What backup utilities come with Windows? Sadly, while other operating systems make backup easy, Microsoft saddles users with a patchwork system of utilities and holdover imaging tools from Windows 7. Some of these work well (Restore Points, File History), others don’t (System Repair Disc, Recovery Drive). None are suitable for quick and easy disaster recovery — even the online backup that is available when you use Windows with a Microsoft cloud account. Thankfully, there are a number of highly capable and far more reliable third-party backup options for Windows that cover the panoply of backup, restore, migration, and disaster recovery. Why you should trust PCWorld for backup software reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name — PCWorld. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware, software, and services for decades. Our backup evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the promises and limitations of every product — from performance to the practicalities of regular use. Backup software powered by AI – EaseUS Todo Backup EaseUS Todo Backup covers everything you need for backups. With AI smart backup, automate your backup tasks on schedule, run to make copies, do realtime protections, and restore everything instantly. No extra effort is required. EaseUS Todo Backup 2026 (Home) – Best overall Windows backup for most PC users - Imaging, backup, sync, and disaster recovery - Occasional non-fatal oddities during file backup and sync Who should buy EaseUS Todo Backup 2026? With a still-affordable perpetual license, it also costs less than some of the now subscription-only competition such as Acronis True Image and Macrium Reflect X. The paid tier of EaseUS is the best all-round home-PC choice for anyone who wants comprehensive backup and recovery with a straightforward “buy once, use forever” license EaseUS Todo Backup 2026: Further considerations Imaging, disaster recovery, plain or compressed file/folder backup, sync, real-time (actually continuous) backup, and nearly every bell and whistle in the backup space are accounted for by Todo Backup. That said, if you want to use EaseUS’s cloud storage (third-party isn’t supported directly), you do need to opt for a yearly plan. Fortunately, it’s decently affordable: software plus 1TB of cloud storage for $60/yr. Acronis True Image – Best comprehensive backup and malware protection - Imaging, backup, and disaster recovery - Actively protects against viruses and ransomware Who should buy Acronis True Image? True Image is a great option for anyone who wants seasoned and reliable file and image backup as well as full-fledged protection from malware (including ransomware). True Image is for users who are amenable to a subscription-only plan, the benefits of which are the iterative and ongoing update potential as well as the inclusion of cloud storage. Acronis established itself as a trustworthy stalwart in backup software years ago. In meantime the program’s moniker morphed for a while to Cyber Protect Home Office (which is actually more descriptive), but is now back again to the more recognizable True Image. Throughout the changes, the program remained super-reliable, and gradually evolved into a versatile, flexible, backup and malware protection solution. Easeus Todo Backup 2025: Further considerations Easeus Todo Backup Free covers all the backup basics: File/folder backup (compressed and plain), one-way sync, system/drive/partition imaging, and all with scheduling. But there are extras you might not expect from a freebie such as backup from network locations, and what EaseUS calls real-time backup (it’s actually continuous — close enough). That’s unique for a freebie. Todo Backup 2025 also sports the easiest, most attractive (in our estimation) interface on the market. That alone should recommend it to most users. There’s a professional version that adds numerous advanced features, as well as EaseUS’s own cloud storage. See the entry above. Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX – Best Windows backup for SMBs - Fast and reliable continuous data protection - Super easy restores to real or virtual hard drives Who should buy Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX? Home, small, and other businesses who are looking for backup software more powerful than the norm, that also scales nicely in networked ecosystems will do well with this solid, feature-laden, and very fast backup program. Besides Arcserve’s support for SMB / mixed Windows-Linux environment, it’s heavy on features that are overkill for most home users, but great for the more robust needs of business users. Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX: Further considerations Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX is loaded with pro- and enterprise-level features including support for third-party virtual hard drives (VHDs, etc.). It is also an excellent choice for Linux users or those in mixed Windows/Linux environments as it’s available for both operating systems. ShadowProtect SPX is a bit pricey, but it’s extremely reliable backup software with foolproof continuous data protection. Note that the company no longer targets the average user, but I found that it works exceptionally well even on a single computer. - Handy Backup Professional: Top-notch features that might’ve garnered a higher rating had it been entirely glitch-free and a bit easier to learn. - NTI Backup Now Pro 7: Another suite that offers a strong feature set — file backup, imaging, continuous and cloud backup — yet is tarnished by glitches. - Ashampoo Backup Pro 27: A great total backup solution for the average user, but a couple features shy of being “pro.” - Paragon Backup & Recovery Community Edition: A free program that offers robust file backup that should meet the needs of most users. - Perfect Backup: Fast and competent, this free backup program is more versatile than Windows File History. - Aomei Backupper Pro: A complete backup solution capable of preserving your important data both locally and remotely. - Aomei Backupper Standard: A respectable free backup program if you can tolerate the occasional ad. - Retrospect 19 Solo: Includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but sadly it lacks disaster recovery. - Retrospect 19 Desktop: The pro version of the above covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price. - Backup and Restore (Windows 7): Conveniently installed with Windows, and good for imaging but bad for disaster recover. - MSP360 Managed Backup: Uses a handy web-based console to provide imaging and file backup services for multiple devices at a reasonable price. - MSP360 Backup: The free incarnation is a worthwhile upgrade to Windows File History. - Iperius Backup: Has power aplenty, but the learning curve and interface might occasionally flummox less-experienced users. - MiniTool ShadowMaker Pro 4.6: There’s a lot to like, particularly its unique ability to interface with all computers on a network. - Macrium Reflect Home: Would likely qualify as our favorite backup software if it wasn’t relatively pricey. It’s an exceptional program that offers everything we want from backup software — full drive/folder backup, ease of use, reliability, etc. - DriveImage XML: A viable free backup solution, albeit only for MBR disks. Note that in this article we focus on local-software based solutions, although many also include a cloud component. For cloud-first backup, see our roundup of the best online backup services. Admittedly, the distinction between the two categories is blurring as they each expand their feature sets. Our reviewers run each program through the various types of backups and restores it’s capable of — including those requiring boot media. This is largely to gauge reliability and hardware compatibility. We check speed, but such is highly reliant upon the connections and media involved. If we notice anything is particularly fast or slow, we’ll tell you about it, but creating a functional backup is paramount. To learn more details, see our article on how PCWorld tests backup software. Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. If you recently purchased an external HDD or SSD from a major vendor such as Seagate or WD, check to see if there are backup utilities or a backup software license included. Whatever backup software you use, keep in mind the following key aspects of the best solutions: file backup for documents/photos, image backup for whole-PC rollback, boot media for dead-drive recovery, versioning for accidental overwrite protection, and know which are critical to your backup plan. If you want to back up your essential data (operating systems and programs can be reinstalled, though it’s mildly time- and effort-consuming), a program that backs up only your important files is essential. Some programs even automatically select the appropriate files or folders. File backup can include operating system files if you wish but is still not suitable for disaster recovery. Images are byte-for-byte snapshots of your entire hard drive (normally not including empty sectors) or partitions, and can be used to restore the operating system, drivers, programs in one swift, fell swoop. Imaging also ensures that you don’t omit anything important as can happen with file backup. Should your system crash completely, you need alternate means to boot your system and restore data using your backup software. Any backup program worth its salt should be able to create a bootable optical disc or USB thumb drive. Some will also create a restore partition on your hard drive, which can be used if the issue isn’t a failed drive. Note that we’ve run into multiple issues with Microsoft’s own Recovery Drive and System repair disc — don’t rely on those. If you’re going to back up effectively, you need to do so on a regular basis. Any backup program you purchase should let you schedule backups and run them in the background. Some even will backup files as they change (real time) or at very short intervals (continuous) Versioning is simply retaining older version of files (or backups) rather than overwriting them during the backup/sync process. You can generally define how many versions to keep, but if you choose to cull older files, this is till not true backup which again, is an immutable copy of your data, drives, or system. Every backup program supports hard drives, but as obsolete as they may seem, DVDs and Blu-Ray discs are great archive media. If you’re worried about optical media’s reliability, M-Disc claims its discs are reliable for a thousand years, backed up by Department of Defense testing. An offsite copy of your data is a hedge against physical disasters such as theft, flood, fire, and power surges. Online storage services are a great way to meet that need. Some backup software will let you back up to Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon S3 and compatible, etc. however Cloud Managers can serve as a workaround with backup programs that don’t. The downside to cloud storage is relatively slow performance. Keep a local backup for faster restores. Backing up to other computers or NAS boxes on your network or in remote locations (say your parent’s or children’s house) is another way of safeguarding your data via a physically remote copy. If you use network storage, it can also be handy to back them up to you local system. FTP/SFTP can be used for offsite, while SMB (Windows and most OS’s) and AFP (Apple) are good for other PCs or NAS on your local network. Network support is not universal, and some backup programs allow you to back up to, but not from network shares. Just be careful in the way you expose your computers on the Internet. Real-time backup means that files are backed up whenever they change, usually upon creation or save. It’s handy for keeping an immediately available backup of rapidly changing data sets. For less volatile data sets, scheduled backups will do just fine. Continuous simply means backing up on a tight schedule, generally every few minutes, rather than in real time, daily, weekly, or monthly. Use continuous backup for rapidly changing data sets where transfer rates are too slow, or computing power too precious for real-time backup. Most backups proceed in the background or during dead time, so performance isn’t a huge issue in the consumer space. However, if you’re backing up multiple machines, backing up to multiple destinations, or dealing with very large data sets, speed will be a consideration. That said, backup speed is highly dependent upon the hardware and transport technology in use. Further reading: Check out PCWorld’s roundup of best external drives for recommendations on reliable storage options — an important component in a comprehensive backup strategy. What is the best Windows backup software? The best Windows backup software is Easeus Todo Backup 2025. It has everything PCWorld expects to see in a top product: A polished interface, intuitive functionality, a comprehensive approach to backing up data including imaging, file backup, sync, and disaster recovery. And most important, it’s reliable! Todo Backup also offers the option of a perpetual license or a subscription model, the latter of which can be augmented with affordable cloud storage. What is the best free Windows backup software? It turns out that PCWorld’s favorite for-pay backup software, Easeus Todo Backup 2025, also offers a surprisingly robust free version. It matches its paid counterpart in basics such as imaging, file backup, sync, and, most especially — disaster recovery. It also features the same eminently user-friendly interface. As with most backup freeware, you will be nagged to upgrade, and Easeus’s optional cloud storage, which is surprisingly affordable, is only available at the subscription tier. Will backup software slow down my computer? Backup software typically runs in the background or during dead time, so given even moderately modern hardware, you shouldn’t notice any decrease in performance. Most programs let you throttle the backup process if you do notice a slowdown. Does Windows Backup and Restore (Windows 7) save everything? Yes, by default, Backup and Restore (Windows 7) saves everything on your system disk (all the partitions, including hidden ones) in what’s known as an image file that would be suitable for disaster recovery if Windows Recovery Drive and Rescue disk were reliable. News bulletin — they aren’t. Hence, we only recommend this program for creating highly compatible VHD/VHDX images of your data drives and partitions which can be mounted as virtual drives and browsed using nothing but Windows Explorer. What’s the difference between Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, etc. and backup software? Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are what’s known as cloud storage, or online storage. They create a local virtual drive that you can drag files to, and which is eventually synced to the cloud as time allows. They also provide a Web portal where you can manage your files remotely. However, by default these services sync changes in the data across all devices. True backups should be immutable snapshots that may be added to but not changed. Some services offer versioning (keeping older files, and adding new ones), which creates a close approximation to backup. Cloud backup services (distinct from those mentioned above) offer many, though not all, of the benefits of Windows backup software. This is generally done with local client software that offers just basic functions like file backup and sync. You can learn more about these in our roundup of best cloud backup services. How often should backups be scheduled? Ideally, as often as your data changes. If you are working on an important project or have work that you absolutely cannot afford to lose, you should consider real time (as data changes) or continuous (very short intervals). Hourly, daily, or longer intervals will be fine for the average user. All file backups should be augmented by weekly or monthly system backups. Can I back up files to and from my cloud storage? Until a few years ago, most Windows backup software was restricted to making local backups — i.e., to another drive, external or internal, connected to your system. There were of course services such as Mozy that had their own backup clients, but that’s covered in our online backup roundup. Here we’re talking just plain backup programs. The situation is improving rapidly, and many backup software vendors are adding online storage services as destinations for their backups. If your favorite backup program doesn’t support cloud storage directly, a cloud storage manager that integrates online storage services into File Explorer can make online backup possible with just about any backup app. What’s the difference between full, differential, and incremental backup? A full backup is a backup of all your data, regardless of how new or old it is. A differential backup is all the data that’s changed since your last full backup. An incremental backup is all the data that’s changed since any your original full and/or the last differential/incremental backup. Differential and incremental backups require a initial full backup to be restored. Differential backups require more time to create than incremental backups, but are quicker to restore since you only need the latest iteration. Differential backups can grow to be quite large if you don’t perform full backups very often. Incremental backups take less time to produce and are smaller, but take longer to restore as all of them created since the last full backup must be restored in the order in which they were created. What’s the difference between image backup, system backup, and file backup? An image is low-level backup of all the sectors (including “empty” sectors if you wish) contained by a disk or partition, regardless of their pertinence to your files. It’s basically fool-proof in terms of accidentally overlooking important data. A system backup is an disk image backup of all the partitions on your system drive. This includes several that are hidden, i.e., not enumerated as drive letters by the operating system. A system backup might also include other drives, but must contain the OS drive. A file backup is a high-level backup of data read via the operating system’s file system. Most often this is data, but may include all the files on a drive. What should I back up? In truth, it’s only your essential personal data that must absolutely, positively, 100% be backed up. Once the family pictures or your work-in-progress are trashed with no backup, there’s no way back other than an expensive recovery service, and even that’s not guaranteed if the physical media is unreadable. On the other hand, a system backup is exceedingly handy for getting you back up to speed with minimal hassle. It returns your system to exactly where you were at the time of the backup: OS, program, updates, upgrades, settings, data are all back in a relative blink of the eye. But it’s not essential. While reinstalling operating systems, drivers, and programs, as well as adjusting settings require more effort, you can then recover your data if that’s all you backed up. See the first paragraph.

item.title: SALES: 7 gadgets that'll instantly upgrade your Thanksgiving feast
item.description:
Source: Engadget
7 gadgets that’ll instantly upgrade your Thanksgiving feast These tools will make turkey day just a little easier. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Thanksgiving is supposed to be a time for rest, relaxation and appreciating all the good things that have happened to you over the past year. However, there's no denying that it's also a ton of work for whoever is in charge of preparing your Thanksgiving meal. Not only do you have to consider the cooking itself, there's all the other things that come with making a holiday feast like choosing the right recipes, gathering all the ingredients and scheduling which dishes need to be cooked at what time so everything is ready together. And all that doesn't even include managing anyone who feels like helping, which can turn into its own logistical issue. So to help smooth out the chaos that is holiday cooking, we've put together a collection of essential cooking gadgets that can save you time and take some of the stress out of preparing your Thanksgiving bounty. Most people probably wouldn't consider a knife to be very techy, and for most blades that sentiment rings true. But on days like Thanksgiving where you're going to be doing a ton of chopping, cutting, slicing and more, it can't hurt to have a little extra help. And then there's the turkey, because it isn't going to carve itself. Furthermore, if you want your bird to look anything like it does in cooking videos with those neat, super clean slices, you're going to need a sharp tool to get there. For cooking nerds who like to geek out about the science of sharpness, one of my favorite knives on the market right now is the Seattle Ultrasonics C-200. In addition to just being a really nice knife featuring a three-layer san mai blade made out of Japanese AUS-10 steel, inside its handle there's a motor that vibrates the knife 30,000 times per second. While the oscillations are so small that you can't actually feel it shaking, those vibrations increased the knife's effective sharpness by up to 50 percent. It excels at delicate foods like tomatoes that often like to stick to the side of your blade, but also denser things like potatoes and meat, which obviously includes turkey. The C-200 even comes with an IP65 rating for dust and water resistance, so there's no worry about ruining its electronics with an errant splash. And if you opt for the wireless charging tile, you'll never have to worry about keeping its battery topped up. Granted, starting at $399, it certainly isn't cheap, but that price is very much in the same range as other premium chef knives from big name companies like Shun, Wusthoff and others. Alternatively, if you want a dedicated gadget for helping you carve a turkey, you can always turn to more traditional electric knives like those from Cusinart, NutriChef, Hamilton Beach and more. Admittedly, these types of knives aren't nearly as pretty as blades like the C200 and the need to plug them in makes them harder to use on an everyday basis. But if you want a relatively easy and affordable way to make serving your Thanksgiving turkey go a bit more smoothly, a classic electric knife is definitely worth a look. Even if you prefer side dishes like mashed potatoes, stuffing or a green bean casserole, there's no denying that the turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner. And if you want it to come out just right, you need a decent thermometer. Not having one is basically gambling that you get lucky with your timing and the bird turns out well. That said, there are a range of options, from simple digital sticks like the affordable ThermoPop 2 to fancy probe thermometers like the second-gen model from Combustion Inc. Basic options require a bit more work as you can't leave them in the bird while it's in the oven, whereas more expensive versions have wireless support that allows you to leave them inside the turkey as it cooks. Some options like those from Combustion Inc. even account for carry-over cooking, which is when the temperature of the food continues to rise even after you take it out of the oven. You just need to decide how much you want to spend and what kind of features you really want. One of my more affordable favorites is the Sense from Chef IQ, which offers a great balance between price and performance. Just don't be a fool and try to rely strictly on the little pop-out thermometers that sometimes come with the bird, as those aren't known for their accuracy or precision. A big issue during Thanksgiving is not having enough room in your oven for everything that needs to be baked or roasted. One easy solution to this is turning to an air fryer, which works almost exactly like the convection function on an oven, but in a smaller volume that's faster to heat and sometimes offers better air circulation. Another really nice thing about air fryers is that they can be quite affordable, with name brand models like the Instant Pot Vortex or the Ninja Air Fryer Pro, both of which are currently going for as little as $80. Upgrading to more expensive fryers like the Philips 3000 can give you more capacity, while even pricier options like the Wonder Oven Pro from Our Place have as many as eight different functions for things like baking, roasting, dehydrating, proofing and more. And perhaps the best thing is that when the holidays are over, you can easily move these into your pantry, closet or garage and reclaim some of your precious kitchen counter space. A good digital scale falls in the same general camp as a decent thermometer and there isn't an experienced baker that would be caught dead without one. They're super easy to use and in my opinion, they are a staple of any well-equipped kitchen. You can just plop a mixing bowl on top, zero out the scale and then add ingredients in as needed while you get precise measurements, which can be especially critical for baked goods and confections. OXO makes a very nice and rather affordable digital scale that starts at around $65, but you can find cheaper options from well-known brands like KitchenAid for barely more than $20. A lot of people think blenders are big, bulky contraptions that make a ton of noise and take up too much room in your kitchen. And while the most powerful ones often are, they don't need to be, as there are affordable options that aren't much bigger than a teapot like these ones from Magic Bullet and Ninja. Regardless, they are great for making a post-dinner milkshake or a lovely fall-inspired soup (butternut squash anyone?). Alternatively, you can opt for an immersion blender (aka a hand blender), which can do much of the same functions as a big countertop model, but gives you even greater control and the ability to blend things directly on the stovetop using the pots you already own. This can make them better choices for whipping up sauces like hollandaise (which is delicious when poured over roasted asparagus), mayonnaise or even a classic cranberry sauce to go with your turkey. I prefer cordless options like those from KitchenAid as they have more than enough battery life to complete multiple dishes and the lack of a wire makes them super easy to use. But if your budget is tight, traditional cabled options are totally fine too and often a more affordable choice. Even for people like me who prefer to chop things by hand, a food processor can be an incredible time saver during the holidays. Not only do they make quick minces of veggies, they can also be used to grate cheese, shred things like potatoes (for an easy Thanksgiving hash), or whip up dips like salsa. Some options like the Cusinart Mini Food processor are stupendously cheap at under $30, while pricer models like the Ninja Professional Plus Food Processor come with a bunch of attachments to handle all sorts of dishes. Cooking food in a water bath might seem like an unnecessarily complex thing to do for the holidays, but it can actually save you time and effort. A good sous vide machine like those from Anova or Breville allow you to set an exact temperature and hold it there almost indefinitely. This allows you to cook things like meat with precision, so there's no worrying about if something is going to come out medium-rare or well-done. And even on Thanksgiving where turkey is the main protein, you can still use a sous vide machine to make dishes like superb rosemary mashed potatoes or luscious glazed carrots. Some models even come with Wi-Fi, so you can start and set them remotely using your phone. On top of that, all they need to function is an outlet, so a sous vide machine can be a great option for people with small kitchens or a limited number of burners on their stove.

item.title: SALES: Top 4 Smart Pergolas for 2027
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
A pergola used to mean wooden slats overhead and crossed fingers whenever clouds rolled in. Smart louvered pergolas change that. Their aluminum roof blades tilt open for sun and breeze or close tight against rain, and you control them from your phone, a remote or your voice. The best ones join the same routines as your smart lights and thermostat, so the roof can close at bedtime or when a storm moves in. Not every smart pergola is equally smart, though. Some work with Alexa, Google Home and Apple Home right out of the box, while others need a separate bridge or hub. Prices run from about $7,500 for a DIY kit to custom builds quoted per project, and installation ranges from a weekend DIY job to a professional crew. We picked four options across those budgets and install types. Whichever you choose, check your local permit rules before you order.
- Buy the Hansø Horizon if you want the best smart pergola overall. - Buy the StruXure Pergola X if your area has strict building codes or permit rules. - Buy the Renson Camargue if you want the most ways to customize the look. - Buy the Azenco R-Blade if you want one pergola to cover a large patio or pool deck.
The Hansø Horizon is the smart pergola we’d recommend to most people, because it gets the smart part right. It works natively with Amazon Alexa, Google Home and Apple HomeKit, so the roof joins the same scenes and routines as the rest of your home without a third-party bridge. Tell your voice assistant goodnight, and the louvers can close and the built-in LED lights dim along with everything else. You can also run it from the app or a remote. Hansø’s Scandinavian design is clean and modern, with double-layer louvers that tilt open for shade or airflow and seal shut against rain. Add Hansø’s rain sensor and the roof closes on its own when a shower starts, even if you’re not home. With Hansø’s Horizon Glass Walls and a heater, the Horizon becomes a proper outdoor room you can use well into the cooler months. Under the clean lines, it’s built to last. The frame uses 6063-T6 aluminum, a stronger temper than the T5 many kits use, and it’s rated for winds up to 165 mph with the louvers closed and snow loads up to 60 PSF. Hansø backs those numbers with a structural engineering report you can request before you buy. The posts sit on SUS304 stainless steel baseplates, and the AkzoNobel powder coat carries its own 7-year finish warranty.
The StruXure Pergola X is the pick if your town is strict about permits. It has an ICC-ES evaluation report (ESR-5321P) showing how it complies with the 2021 International Building Code, the kind of paperwork building officials look for, and StruXure says it’s the only louvered pergola maker with ICC certification. Each Pergola X is also built to order in the U.S. for its project. The report has limits, though: it doesn’t cover areas in higher seismic design categories, which include much of the West Coast, so confirm with your building department before you count on it. The Pergola X runs on Somfy motors, and the StruXure Bridge, powered by Bond, adds app control, schedules and voice control through Alexa, Google Home or Control4. A universal remote and a post-mounted control cover the times you’d rather not reach for your phone. Sizing is fully custom, and the lifetime system warranty can be transferred to the next owner if you sell your home. The catch is price and process. StruXure doesn’t publish prices, because a local dealer designs, quotes and installs each project, so expect to pay well above kit prices. It’s the right choice when budget isn’t the main concern and you want a code-evaluated structure handled by one dealer from design through installation.
The Renson Camargue is the pick if you care how every detail looks. Its aluminum comes in any RAL color or a wood-look finish, and you can choose translucent roof blades that let daylight through even when the roof is closed. The blades tilt up to 150 degrees, and each Camargue is made to measure, either freestanding or mounted against your house. Renson’s side elements follow the same idea, from sliding glass panels and aluminum walls to wood-look Loggia sun panels and outdoor curtains in 12 colors. You can control the roof, screens, lighting and heating through the Renson Connect app, a Somfy remote or a wall switch. The app needs a Somfy TaHoma hub in your home, so factor that into setup. Like StruXure, Renson sells through certified dealers who quote and install each project, so this isn’t a weekend DIY build. It’s best for design-led projects where the finished look matters more than speed or price.
The Azenco R-Blade can do in one zone what might take two kits elsewhere, which makes it a natural fit for a big pool deck or rooftop. A single R-Blade zone spans up to 22 feet 10 inches by 16 feet. Its motorized louvers pair with a Bond Bridge Pro for app control on iPhone or Android and voice control through Alexa, Google Home, Siri or Control4, and the dual-wall blades are built for strength. Azenco designs the R-Blade for tough climates, and it holds Miami-Dade Notice of Acceptance (NOA) certification. To keep that certification valid, Azenco-certified professionals must install it, and pricing comes through dealers by quote. That makes the R-Blade a high-end, hired-crew project and more than a small patio needs. When you have a lot of ground to cover, though, it’s hard to beat.
A pergola that works natively with Alexa, Google Home and Apple Home can join your existing routines, while one that relies on a remote or a dealer-installed hub stays more of a standalone gadget. We gave the most weight to native voice-assistant support and app control. Wind and snow ratings only mean something if there’s engineering behind them. We favored brands that back their numbers with a structural report or a building-code certification over a figure printed on a product page. Some pergolas arrive as kits you can assemble over a weekend, while others are designed, quoted and installed by a dealer. Made-to-order models also take longer to arrive, so we noted the wait wherever it matters. We compared regular prices rather than sale prices, and looked at what each warranty actually covers: the structure, the finish and the motor and electronics.
What makes a pergola smart? A smart pergola has motorized louvers you can control from an app, a voice assistant or an automation, not just a hand crank or a remote. The smartest models can also react to the weather, closing the roof when a rain sensor detects a shower. Do I need a permit for a louvered pergola? Often, depending on its size and your local building code. Ask the brand for its engineering documents before you order, since your building department may want to see them. Can a smart pergola close itself when it rains? Yes, with a rain sensor. The Hansø Horizon offers one as an add-on that closes the louvers automatically when rain starts.

item.title: SALES: Amazon Kindle (2026) vs. Kindle Paperwhite (2026): Should you pay more for your e-reader?

The 2026 Kindle comes in four shades: Graphite and Ube (16GB version) and Alpine Sky Aluminum and Seaglass Green Aluminum (32GB). Translated, that’s black, soft purple, soft blue, and light green. item.title: SALES: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful. Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island. Grace Bay, Providenciales — Turks & Caicos Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.) The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here. A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable. Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants. If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind. The Baths National Park, Virgin Gorda — British Virgin Islands There are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling. Tropic of Cancer Beach, Little Exuma — Bahamas The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights. A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi. The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest. While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

item.title: SALES: The best tiramisu in London right now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Rich yet light, bitter but sweet and with just enough of a boozy coffee hit that picks you up after a hearty Italian meal, the best tiramisu in London are balanced to perfection, whether they're classic espresso-soaked slabs, in doughnut form – or even vegan. “It's not the taste of coffee or the taste of cocoa, or the taste of mascarpone or ladyfingers or eggs. No, it's the result of all these ingredients together, the balance of these ingredients,” explains Tiramisu World Cup founder Francesco Redi. Some of London's loveliest Italian restaurants have naturally perfected a traditional take on the creamy Italian pick-me-up, while some others are going in on playful twists of the classic that are really, really worth saving room for. Here, we have wiped dessert plates clean on a quest to find the very best places to go for London's tastiest tiramisu. - Best family-style serving: Rosina, Wandsworth - Best alternative tiramisu: Burro, Covent Garden How we chose the best tiramisu in London The best tiramisu in London are from places across the capital which our editors and writers rate most for the Italian dessert. All of the restaurants listed below have been tried (many times) by our team, and rank highly for their take on tiramisu. For more foodie recommendations, see our guides: When it comes to Highbury’s Lupa, what this butter-yellow restaurant lacks in size, it more than makes up for in reputation. Co-owned by actor Theo James and Ed Templeton of Carousel and with a kitchen helmed by the talented Naz Hassan, this little neighbourhood joint has become a North London cornerstone, and for good reason. The menu is Roman-inspired (aka comforting to the max), with a delightfully no-holds-barred approach to its use of ingredients. One of the menu staples, the classic tiramisu, is no exception. More mascarpone? More espresso? More booze? No problem. The perfect finishing touch after multiple courses of pasta and succulent meats, the tiramisu’s coffee hit immediately cut through the richness, while its layers of creamy mascarpone were positively cloud-like. The portion may have seemed intimidating at first, yet somehow we were left scraping the sides of the bowl for the final lashings of the dessert. Lucy Bruton Address: Lupa, 73 Highbury Park, London N5 1UA Purists, look away. Burro – or butter, in Italian – certainly lives up to its name. Connor Gadd (from much-loved Highbury restaurant Trullo) opened his first solo venture in Covent Garden's Floral Court to serve up generous and indulgent modern Italian cooking to central Londoners. For antipasti and primi, you'll find comforting dishes like rabbit crocchette, duck ragu fettuccine and pici with slow-cooked tomato and basil on the menu. The tiramisu doughnuts were the highlight on the day I visited, and made dessert a bit of a speed match between my fellow diner and me to see who could inhale these ricotta-laced balls of joy the fastest. Baked to order, you get the best of tiramisu flavours in spherical form – coated with sugar and crushed ladyfingers – and piled high over coffee cream and Marsala. Address: 2 Floral Court, Floral Street, Covent Garden, London WC2E 9FB. It's all about Italian food with distinctive layers at Tom's Pasta, the supper-club-like Italian restaurant hidden away inside a leafy terrace dotted with artist studios by Hackney Downs. The Hackney trattoria is much loved for its gargantuan beef shin lasagne, piled high with indulgent layers of pasta and ragu and topped with what some might call an obscene amount of parmesan shavings. The classic tiramisu is well worth the visit, too. It's soft and bitter with just the right level of sweet to cut through the indulgent mains – and big enough to share between two. Finish your hearty meal with an aperitif on the terrace. Address: Hackney Downs Studios, 17 Amhurst Terrace, London, E8 2BT Café Petiole at Somerset House, Covent Garden Somerset House is brimming with excellent food options, from Aram by Imad for Syrian flavours to Poon's for Chinese cooking and the late Skye Gyngell's Spring for sustainably-minded British fine-dining (museum restaurants have come a long way!). For vegans, Café Petiole by Tendril's Rishim Sachdeva is a no-brainer for daytime dining. Set in a beautiful pastel-hued space with dusky pink tables, Café Petiole's salads and sandwiches make it one of the best and most beautiful places for a quick and healthy lunch in the area. It's the Tendril Tiramisu, though, a vegan twist on classic tiramisu that'll really blow your mind for Sachdeva's genius way with plant-based food. Address: Somerset House, Strand, London, WC2R 1LA It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Tiramisu here comes from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF Whether you’re looking for a cosy date-night spot or a lively dinner with friends, there’s a reason Leo’s is drawing Londoners to this quiet corner of Lower Clapton. It may look like a retro East London cafe from the outside, but don’t be fooled – tucked away in a back room of Leo’s is a bright and airy bistro-style dining room complete with white tablecloths and mid-century-style wooden panelling. The menu pays homage to chef Peppe’s Sardinian heritage. The tiramisu here is such a hit that it's made its way to the breakfast menu, too. The perfectly constructed thick slab is utterly decadent and worth travelling all across London for, with chocolate nibs on the bottom and soaked in their in-house coffee. Lucy Bruton Address: 59 Chatsworth Road, London, United Kingdom E5 0LH Creamy, boozy and not too sweet, the tiramisu at Senza Fondo in Shoreditch is well worth stretching the stomach for, which you will likely need at this all-you-can-eat lasagne spot in Shoreditch. Despite lunch feeling a little like extreme eating, this would be a wonderful spot to bring family and friends. The interior feels like a family-owned Italian spot – all red checked tablecloths and pictures of diners on the walls – while the staff are warm and let you take your time over the huge portions. Abigail Malbon Don't be fooled by the glitzy Mayfair postcode; the menu at Bar Finch is a triumph of Italian-tinged comfort food. Portion sizes across the whole menu are perfect for sharing (and actually so – not just billed that way on the menu only to arrive disappointingly tiny). The grandest of them all? The tiramisu, which is utterly huge and soaked in booze in the best way. This is a delightful spot to hunker down on a cold and gloomy evening at leisure. There’s no need to rush away so soon. Charley Ward Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei, Embankment It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. The showstopping tiramisu at this A-list loved spot is presented to the table in a family-style bowl; the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ “We wanted to make somewhere we dreamed of eating at”, co-founder Mario Carbone told Condé Nast Traveller’s digital editor Sarah James when she was granted early access to his eponymous restaurant. He’s not alone, as it's clear that most of London dreamt of eating here, too. Carbone NYC has long been synonymous with A-listers and fashionable figures, with mere mortal foodies refreshing their emails in anticipation of securing a coveted reservation and it's a similar show this side of the pond. Showmanship is certainly the name of the game at Carbone, especially when it comes to desserts. The gargantuan Stracciatella Tiramisu is the only way to end a meal here, appearing hedgehog-like in a large bowl on a silver platter. When Simonetta Wenkert and her husband Avi took over the premises, they were uncertain that it would be a success. These days, getting a table is a competitive sport. It is, Simonetta says, the most romantic restaurant in London – and we're predisposed to agree. Tiny tables jostle for space in the candlelit dining room, with its retro posters and half-open kitchen. Recipes come from owner Avi’s mother, a home cook born in a hilltop town near Perugia, for whom the restaurant is named. A completely comforting spot for a classic tiramisu. Sarah James Address: Ida, 222a Kilburn Lane, Queen's Park, London W10 4AT

item.title: SALES: 17 best libraries in London for bookworms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Walk around London and there’s no shortage of signs that the capital city has long played host to some of the world’s greatest authors, providing the backdrop to their books. From Hampstead blue plaques showing the former abodes of John Keats and Rabindranath Tagore to Monica Ali’s Brick Lane and Zadie Smith’s beloved NW2, there is no shortage of inspiration to be found in London’s literary haunts. But when it comes to cosying up with a good book on a rainy day, where should bookworms go? One of the best libraries in London, of course. There are the standouts: The British Library is suitably grand and impressive but if you’re looking for something more niche, whether it’s foreign-language children’s books, poetry readings, or the world’s smallest copy of Dante’s The Divine Comedy, these bookish buildings offer plenty for bibliophiles. Beginning life at Burlington Gardens in Piccadilly, the University of London Library took up residence in 1937 in an imposing 19-floor Art Deco building in leafy Bloomsbury, designed by Charles Holden. During WWII, Senate House contained the headquarters for the Ministry of Information, where George Orwell’s wife, Eileen Blair, just so happened to be employed in the censorship department that inspired 1984. There is still a rare first edition from 1949 and even a Room 101, now used for private events. Open to the public as well as students, the library’s two million books are spread across 15 floors, which feature six historic reading rooms and 52 special collections containing everything from full-page illustrations by Terry Pratchett to 700 items owned by Walter de la Mare. Known for promoting radical politics and social justice, the library includes an exhibition space and is currently hosting A Place to Call Home: Poverty and Housing in London, charting the cultural, economic and political history of the capital over the past 200 years. Address: Senate House Library, Malet Street, London WC1E 7HU Website: london.ac.uk/senate-house-library 2. Bibliothèque Quentin Blake, Institut Français After major refurbishment, the Children’s Library of the Institut Français was renamed and reopened in September 2015 as the Bibliothèque Quentin Blake, in homage to the beloved illustrator. Now twice as big – and twice as beautiful – the free-entry French-language library holds all the greats from René Goscinny and Hergé to Serge Bloch and Dominique de Saint Mars. Wooden-floored and stacked with colourful cube-shaped shelves, comic books and board games, the library zings with bookish energy for children up to the age of 12. A soft-pink wall hanging, commissioned specially for the library, features a mass of children, birds and adults sitting in trees devouring books, and exudes Blake’s familiar vim and vigour. One glance is all you need to want to gather every book in sight and rush home to devour them all. Address: Bibiliothèque Quentin Blake, 32 Harrington Road, London SW7 3ES Entering the doors of the UK’s national library, it’s hard not to feel studious within this huge, light-filled foyer – even if you’re only there for a quick espresso, a slab of chocolate cake or a roam around the major new exhibition Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery which runs until the end of June 2027. Famous for its astounding collection of manuscripts, maps, musical recordings and newspapers dating back to the 1600s, the red-brick building shaped like a cruise liner holds two original copies of Magna Carta, the illustrated manuscript of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland that Lewis Carroll presented to Alice Liddell in November 1864, and the earliest surviving copy of Beowulf. Once a favourite of authors looking for a quiet place to write, the library has recently come under fire for proposing to hand over three of its 11 public reading rooms as business places for hire. However, a petition launched by the Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union calling for a halt to the move has gathered more than 17,000 signatures. Watch this space. Address: The British Library, 96 Euston Road, London NW1 2DB Housed inside an old phone box, the city’s smallest library was created by one-time Lewisham resident, Sebastian Handley, who reportedly bought the phone box for £1 as part of BT’s Adopt a Kiosk scheme. Spending around £500 to install eight shelves and polish it up, Handley trusted the library to local residents who have managed the bright red corner of delight on Loampit Hill for more than 12 years with remarkable community spirit, borrowing books – and bringing them back. Anyone is welcome to donate their own unwanted travel books, novels, guide books and thrillers with authors ranging from Jojo Moyes and Hanif Kureishi to Uketsu and Amy Abdelnoor crammed in on every shelf. Address: Corner of Lewisham Way/Tyrwhitt Road, Lewisham, London SE4 1XL Overlooking the Thames on the fifth floor of the Royal Festival Hall is the National Poetry Library, a warm yellow glow radiating through the double doors. Opened in 1953 by T.S. Eliot and Herbert Read, the library now contains more than 200,000 works of modern British poetry and offers a cosy space in which emerging poets can seek advice, thumb through battered copies of Larkin, Hughes and Plath, or simply sit in quietude as visiting poets read their work in front of the huge, rainbow-coloured archives. For budding poets, there’s also the Little Library where children can pore over picture books, play games and solve puzzles or enjoy Friday-morning Rug Rhymes events when the library’s puppets, Firebird and Federico, share some of their favourite poems and stories with little ones under five. Address: National Poetry Library, Southbank Centre, Belvedere Road, London SE1 8XX With its polished wooden rails, thick red carpets and sage-looking busts in the corners, one could be forgiven for thinking the library is as traditional as they come. Not so. Located just off St James’s Square, the London Library offers members access to more than a million books while also hosting author talks and an emerging writers programme now entering its seventh year. Amid the special collections are the world’s smallest version of Dante’s The Divine Comedy and a first edition of Martin Luther’s 1522 translation of the New Testament into German. However, no visit is complete without the thrill of nosing around the bookstacks, which span 17 miles of shelving, nothing more than iron-grille flooring in between. Address: 14 St James’s Square, London SW1Y 4LG An extension of the Wellcome Collection, which focuses on health and the human experience, the library is a dream for readers fascinated by the mind, mental health and medicine across the ages. Spread across two floors on shelves painted with limbs and organs, there are books on everything from sperm counts, transitioning and virility to cosmetic surgery in China, the importance of suffering and the history of waxworks. The main gallery isn’t strictly part of the library but it does carry many of its books. With a warning that it contains human remains, the entrance leads visitors into a warmly lit space hung with lamps on red ropes where solitary readers are concealed in corners and a small wall of handwritten notes asks children to continue each other’s stories. A perfect spot for a rainy day. Address: The Wellcome Library, 183 Euston Road, London NW1 2BE A cultural space in Fitzrovia that opened towards the end of 2025, Ibraaz is a warm and welcoming hub centring dialogue and ideas from North Africa, the Middle East and the global majority. Spanning five floors with a bookshop, a Tunisian café, a performance room and workshop, it offers library residencies on rotation with the Earshot Library-in-Residence currently in situ. In an airy second-floor room with a wooden floor hangs a transparent curtain onto which a pale violet light is projected. Speakers placed around the room create an immersive audio experience drawn from Earshot’s field recordings which investigate noise pollution and ecological damage, and ambient recordings submitted for forensic analysis. Visitors are invited to sit at three computers at the front of the room, each of which has a headset to wear to interact with AI-generated voices and audio deepfakes; audio ballistic analysis of drones; and Earshot’s techniques for profiling sounds and soliciting earwitness testimony of notable events. A profound and impactful experience. It’s the drawing room we all dream of having, one that’s wrapped in bookshelves. With her signature fabric, Firmdale’s Kit Kemp has covered the walls with textured oak leaves in rich reds, golds and greens, lampshades sit on painted ladders and pale wooden floors allow the colours of patterned upholstery to pop. Floor-to-ceiling curtains in the same Falling Leaves fabric lend warmth to this glorious library which has seven shelves of multi-coloured books running around the room. And of course, there’s a rolling ladder to allow hotel guests to clamber up and search the sections for whatever suits their fancy among the 4,500 hardbacks, all of which have had their jackets removed to reveal coloured soft-cloth surfaces with shiny foils and embossed titles. If that wasn’t enough, there’s an honesty bar tucked into a tiny side room with bags of crisps, Hayman’s gin and a fridge full of Krug. Address: Ham Yard Hotel, 1 Ham Yard, W1D 7DT Keen to make clear they’re a bar first and a library second, The Library Lounge at the Standard Hotel in King’s Cross feels much like walking into the 1970s with its orange, squishy leather sofas, walls as furry as carpets and a DJ booth that plays host to podcast recordings, poetry readings and even book launches. In 2019 the hotel opened on the site of the old Camden Town Hall Annex, with the design team hiring a curator whose job it was to search out books from second-hand bookshops, eBay and online sellers whose covers and spines would characterise the 70s and 80s at first glance. Shelves are organised and tagged as Darkness and Light, Chaos and Order, and Politics and Tragedy, and all the books are stickered and logged like regular library books. There’s also a standalone shelf for pets. So if you’ve ever wondered about Breaking Bad Habits in Parrots, All About Goats or needed to get your hands on The Greyhound Owners Encyclopaedia, then come down to Argyle Street and settle in. But you’ll have to buy a drink first. Few collections have ever moved house as often as the women’s library, which officially opened as the Women’s Service Library in 1926. From the outset, it was established to serve two agendas: preserving the history of the women’s suffrage movement, and to offer resources for newly-enfranchised women to take their place in public life. The collection was gradually built from donations, with letters being sent out to authors to ask them to send in their books. During World War II the collection was hastily transferred to Oxford but has finally come to rest at its permanent home since 2013 at the London School of Economics, where it thrives as the oldest and largest library in Britain devoted to the history of women’s campaigning and activism. Address: School of Economics and Political Science, Houghton St, London WC2A 2AE 12. The Maughan Library, King’s College London Whether you’re standing on the grass outside looking in, or gazing up from a lamp-lit desk, the 19th-century Neo-Gothic dome of the Maughan library’s Round Reading room is as hypnotic as it is beautiful. Based on the British Museum’s own Round Reading Room, the former headquarters of the Public Record Office was acquired by King’s College London in 1998 which invested £40m to transform the building into the library. One of the locations referenced by Robert Langdon in the book of The Da Vinci Code, the Maughan stocks theses, journals, exam papers and books on humanities, science and law. It also houses a former medieval chapel now known as the Weston Room, complete with stained-glass windows and a mosaic floor that echoes with careful footsteps. Address: The Maughan Library, Chancery Lane, London WC2A 1LR 13. National Art Library, Victoria & Albert Museum The future of the National Art Library came into question in 2021 after the director of the V&A announced restructuring plans that would cut staff and restrict access to the collection. Currently one of the world’s top art libraries, it overlooks the John Madejski Garden at the V&A and houses a general collection on ceramics, textiles, art, sculpture and fashion – including hundreds of back editions of Vogue – and a special collection that includes Dickens’s original manuscripts and several corrected proofs such as Bleak House. Majestic and redolent with the smell of dust and worn leather, the library is one to visit as soon as you can. Address: National Art Library, V&A, Cromwell Road, London SW7 2RL From across the water, the library resembles a concrete ship that’s run aground. But what it lacks in aesthetics it more than makes up for in spirit and ethos: the construction incorporates ground-source heat pumps, solar-heating panels and a sedum green roof along with responsibly sourced timber. And the inside is more than a library but a lifeline for the local community where children can learn to code, older members can seek help with job-hunting and others can enjoy mystery book bags that introduce readers to genres they wouldn’t normally try. With checked carpets, sleek wood interiors and suspended giant orb lights, it's a wonderful space to while away the day. Address: Canada Water Library, 21 Surrey Quays Road, London SE16 7AR Peckham Library's steel and concrete design won the Stirling Prize for its ground-breaking architecture in 2000. Since then, it's become a hub of community activity – there are book groups for adults, including a group focused on literature from Black authors once a month, as well as classes such as Rhymetime and craft clubs for kids. Three timber-clad pods which look like treehouses make the main reading room eclectic and whimsical – much like the neighbourhood itself – and there are great views across Peckham from the upper floors. Address: Peckham Library, 122 Peckham Hill Street, London SE15 5JR Open to everyone, free of charge, the Reuben Library at BFI is perhaps unsurprisingly dedicated to texts on film, television and the moving image, mainly spotlighting British works but with some international references woven through. The Edwin Fox Foundation Reading Room has study areas, drop-in areas for group projects and scanners so you can digitise your research. There's also a calendar of events that take place here: think discussions on children's television or panels about specific bodies of work, such as Star Wars (note that the library only seats 50, and most events do sell out, so be sure to book in advance). Address: BFI Reuben Library, Belvedere Road, London SE1 8XT Housed in a Grade II-listed terrace on leafy Russell Square, the Wiener Holocaust Library is one of the world’s leading archives of the period, holding works that pre-date the Holocaust. Founded in 1933 by Dr Alfred Wiener, it has a collection of 1,300 testimonies taken during the Holocaust as well as documents relating to the 1938 November Pogrom. It’s a quiet airy space, with maps of the death marches displayed on the ground level along with original letters written in 1949 by children searching for parents sent to the concentration camps. Up the stairs, visitors are greeted by a touching wall of honour to memorialise a loved one who has inspired them. In addition to an extensive collection of books on refugees, genocide and war criminals, the second floor also holds examples of propaganda, an 18th-century Torah scroll saved from destruction in Prague and private reading desks. An independent charity, the free public library is open four days a week and funded entirely by private donors. Address: The Wiener Holocaust Library, 29 Russell Square, London WC1B 5DP

item.title: SALES: Peppermint Mocha Pistachio Milk, Olive Wood Steak Knives, and More Things BA Editors Loved in November
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. Between our own purchases and the endless stream of samples sent our way, it means there’s always something new coming across our desks and into our homes. Each month we round up the standouts we tested or bought ourselves that changed the way we cook and eat. This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea. Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November. This summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor What is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager Waterdrop M6CG Hot & Cold Reverse Osmosis System There were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of New Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on big sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive new flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table. Enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently launched a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I quickly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice. The sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy
